#9808. Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+

So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

The observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:

Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

These results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:

No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++

A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½)

Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.

Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training. The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are:

Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv. You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency.

The public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark.

Keep the three repositories side by side:

The released stack targets Linux, Python 3.12, Verl 0.9.0, and the pinned package lock:

The final two commands should report a verified patched Verl checkout and no broken requirements. Do not run another automatic package sync afterward: it can replace the patched source installation with the vanilla Verl wheel.

Start with the publicly provided samples, or add your own authorized dataset in ThinkingBox format. Then run the repository's preparation script:

The script aggregates policy probes, applies offline policy-relative difficulty filters and benchmark exclusions, and writes the selected train.yaml and test.yaml files. docs/data-preparation.md documents the input fields, loader contract, and complete command.

Follow docs/reference-q38-run.md to start Typesense and the MCP servers, configure the simulated user and judge, set the model, task-list, checkpoint, and topology variables, and prepare the Ray cluster. Keep credentials in runtime secret injection rather than committed files or shell history.

Before allocating a training job, use the guide's dry-run command:

It must exit zero without starting Ray or allocating GPUs. Read the emitted python -m verl.trainer.main_ppo command and every resolved override before launching the run.

The launcher configures training; it does not provision hosts. On the reference three-node topology, export the same environment on every node, mount CHECKPOINT_DIR at the same absolute path, then start Ray:

After ray status reports all 24 GPUs, launch once from the head node:

The first ThinkingBox post covers Typesense, the MCP Session Proxy, and OpenEnv setup. Merge the trained checkpoint following docs/evaluation.md, then serve it with vLLM.

From the OpenEnv repository root, set MERGED_MODEL to the merged model directory and THINKINGBOX_DATA to the pinned benchmark checkout. The historical checkpoint evaluation used this eight-A100 serving configuration:

In a separate terminal, start the OpenEnv compatibility proxy for the Qwen chat template from the ThinkingBox Training checkout. It listens on port 8014 and forwards to vLLM on 8001:

Keep it running during evaluation. From another terminal, check readiness:

Update the agent entry in the existing thinkingbox.yaml; retain its MCP, simulated-user, and judge configuration:

Start OpenEnv as in the first post, with OPENENV_TB_CONFIG pointing to this thinkingbox.yaml and OPENENV_TB_DATASET to $THINKINGBOX_DATA. Once /ready succeeds, run the full protocol of 507 tasks × 20 attempts:

The full profile validates all 10,140 expected task/repetition keys before aggregation.

The useful part of this work is not one Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. It is the training loop and training data curation that turns executable outcomes into rewards.

If you are training or evaluating an agent that touches real database records:

Further details can be found in the following links:

ThinkingBox code is MIT-licensed; the benchmark data is CDLA-Permissive-2.0.

#9807. Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

Discovered using AI, the memory corruption vulnerability affects the OpenJDK runtime and could allow unauthenticated attackers to take over systems.

A critical flaw in an open source runtime at the heart of the Java programming language allows unauthenticated attackers to perform remote code execution (RCE) on myriad Java applications used globally across enterprise organizations.

The memory corruption vulnerability exists in versions of OpenJDK, a popular open source runtime. Researchers at security startup Calif demonstrated a general proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for the flaw, dubbed "Java4Shell" and discovered with the help of artificial intelligence (AI), according to a report published Tuesday.

However, they are holding back the release of "weaponized chains for individual products" to give organizations time to upgrade to patch the vulnerability, officially tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and rated as 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, in affected applications, Calif security engineer Quang Luong wrote in the post.

Java4Shell affects the following releases: Java 17: 17.0.6 to 17.0.21; Java 21: up to 21.0.13 affected; Java 25: up to 25.0.5; Java 27: up to 27.0.1; Java 8, 8u511b33-perf, its Performance Pack build. Java 11 and Java 17.0.0 to 17.0.5 remain unaffected.

Related:'God Mode' Flaws Could Wreak Border-Control Havoc

OpenJDK published a security advisory on the flaw, and Oracle released a patch yesterday to fix the issue in the affected versions of Java. "All Java users should update immediately," Luong recommended.

The flaw exists because of how OpenJDK decodes Base64, a common way of representing binary data as text in authentication protocols, in file uploads, and to deliver network messages.

"To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once," Luong explained. "We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory."

Specifically, OpenJDK uses specialized AVX-512 VBMI instructions on supported x86-64 processors, he explained. The bug is present in the hand-rolled assembly code that handles the final few characters.

"For the 65-character input above, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte result array," Luong wrote. "After decoding the first 64 characters, the routine mishandles the stray = and calculates a negative output length. That invalid length becomes a full 64-byte write, sending 62 bytes past the end of the array."

Java eventually rejects the input, but by then neighboring objects may already be corrupted, he added. Thus, attackers can exploit the bug to reveal sensitive memory, as the highly critical OpenSSL flaw Heartbleed did in 2014, or to perform RCE. "The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:," Luong wrote.

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

Much like previous high-profile flaws before it, including not only Heartbleed but also PHP2Shell and Log4Shell, the flaw has potential to create a security quagmire across entire technology ecosystems because of how widespread the use of the vulnerable software component is. Indeed, Java "is the beating heart of the modern economy" and the third most popular programming language, powering 90% of Fortune 500 companies, Luong wrote.

Log4Shell, disclosed in 2021, affected Apache Log4j, a commonly used Java logging library, and enabled attackers to execute malicious code remotely. More recently, PHP2Shell, disclosed in October 2026, exposed critical vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on vulnerable servers.

Fortunately for defenders, Java4Shell should not quite have the impact that Log4Shell did and still does, though it doesn't mean they shouldn't take Java4Shell very seriously, Duong tells Dark Reading.

"Log4Shell was very easy to exploit," he says. "Java4Shell [is] harder. However, we're comparing a 10 to a 9. They are both very bad; Log4Shell was just worse."

Related:Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Both flaws also highlight the difficulty of identifying vulnerable components hidden within applications and third-party software used across organizations; Java4Shell is similar in this respect because it gives attackers a direct route to enterprise environments through otherwise trusted apps.

"Java4Shell is a reminder that the software underneath your applications is also your attack surface," observes Dom Glavach, CISO at application security solutions provider Black Duck.

The practical problem now for organizations "is that exposure depends on the Java build, the processor and how an application handles input, and many teams cannot answer those questions quickly, especially for JDKs bundled inside applications and containers," he says.

Because flaws like these are so deeply embedded, they may go undiscovered and remain critical security gaps. In this case, the use of AI to uncover Java4Shell potentially may have helped the industry avert disaster, giving organizations time to patch before it's been widely exploited, notes James Matchett, head of security at Cloudsmith.

"Its discovery shows how AI can uncover weaknesses in widely used software that might otherwise have gone undetected for years," he says.

Indeed, Java4Shell's discovery iillustrates how AI can speed up vulnerability discovery.

"An AI coding assistant found this bug in about an hour and a first working exploit took two more, for under $200 in tokens," Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering for cybersecurity firm Secure.com, tells Dark Reading. "The flaw sat in one of the most-audited runtimes there is. That is what discovery looks like now: cheap, fast, and available to defenders and attackers alike."

However, Matchett says the flip side is it also can help attackers move more quickly to weaponize security flaws, noting that organizations are under intense pressure to find and remediate vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them. As Ahmed puts it, "defenders now have less time between a bug being found and being used."

There is little doubt that defenders should take the Java4Shell seriously. Calif researchers demonstrated RCE in a laundry list of widely deployed Java applications in their default configurations, noting that they, too, used AI to develop exploits, Luong wrote.

The team achieved pre-authorization RCE in the following: Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Meanwhile, Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker are vulnerable to post-auth RCE, they said.

"The lists are non-exhaustive," Luong wrote. "We also demonstrated RCE in sample applications built on widely used frameworks, including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Ordinary features such as authentication and file uploads can expose the vulnerable Base64 decoder, extending the potential impact far beyond the products we tested."

An independent researcher also shared with Calif a client-side exploit that demonstrates how "a Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own," Luong wrote.

As mentioned, organizations should start mitigations as soon as possible, with patching Internet-facing applications as the top priority, and internal apps second, Luong tells Dark Reading. Calif will wait at least one-to-two weeks before releasing any app-specific exploit code to allow for defenders to upgrade.

"Thanksgiving is also coming, [and] everyone needs a break," he says.

Organizations also can mitigate Java4Shell by starting OpenJDK with one of the following flags: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable hardware-accelerated Base64 encoding and decoding, or -XX:UseAVX=2 to disable AVX-512, Luong advised.

The second should only be applied on x86-64 hosts, as OpenJDK on ARM does not recognize it and thus won't start the system, he added.

Black Duck's Glavach recommends that organizations start their mitigation process with conducting an inventory, patching Internet-facing identity and build systems first, and staying clear of unverified fixes and fake exploits circulating online.

Secure.com's Ahmed was even more specific, advising that organizations "find every server running Java 17.0.6 or later, patch the ones open to the Internet first, and turn off the Base64 intrinsic where you can't patch yet."

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9806. AttackIQ Research Reveals How Iranian Cyber Groups Hand Off Network Access to Enable Destructive Attacks

Analysis of 20 Iranian state-sponsored threat groups details how espionage, ransomware, and hacktivism intersect in state-backed cyber campaigns.

ANTA CLARA, Calif. — (BUSINESS WIRE) — AttackIQ, the leader in threat-informed Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM), today released new research that connects previously fragmented reporting on individual Iranian cyber campaigns to map the relationships among state-sponsored operators and the institutions supporting them. The findings show Iranian espionage groups turn compromised networks into launchpads for other operators, transforming intelligence-gathering operations into destructive attacks.

Threat reporting on Iran typically covers one campaign at a time, and vendors track the same groups under different names. Helix Kitten alone appears under eight other names, including OilRig, APT34 and Scarred Manticore. AttackIQ’s Adversary Research Team consolidated that reporting into Weighing Cyber Power: Evaluating the Strategic and Operational Significance of Iran’s State-Sponsored Cyber Capability, a single map of 20 Iranian adversaries, the government institutions they are linked to and the contractors that supply their personnel, tooling and infrastructure.

Related:Attackers Target .NET Developers With Poisoned Job Assessments

“The value of threat research is measured by the decisions it informs,” said Paul Reid, VP of Adversary Research at AttackIQ. “Understanding which Iranian groups work together, and how confident we can be in each relationship, gives defenders a clear starting point for emulation and a realistic picture of what could follow an initial compromise. It turns a single detection into a forecast of what comes next.”

The report traces how a single intrusion can pass between groups. In one documented case, Helix Kitten (Scarred Manticore), conducted prolonged intelligence collection inside a network before handing off the network access to Banished Kitten (Void Manticore), which pursued destructive objectives. In a second case, Static Kitten (Mango Sandstorm) established access and passed it to Storm-1084, a destructive operator. In a separate campaign against the Albanian government, four separately tracked groups contributed to the same operation, which spanned reconnaissance, initial access, data theft and the deployment of destructive tooling.

When the damage arrives, it is frequently disguised. The research also found Iranian groups staging destructive attacks as ransomware or hacktivism, obscuring the intent behind the attacks. Pioneer Kitten provided criminal ransomware affiliates with access to compromised networks.

The organizations hit first may be a route to other targets. Several groups can gain access to more heavily defended organizations, including in the defense industrial base, through their subsidiaries, contractors, and suppliers.

Related:Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge

The analysis classifies 20 Iranian adversaries into three weight classes based on their organizational significance, operational relevance, and demonstrated capabilities. The classifications underscore that even smaller, specialized groups can play critical roles in larger cyber campaigns.

Heavyweight: Established groups with sustained espionage operations, internally developed tooling and a central role in Iran’s cyber strategy.

Lightweight: Groups with more focused missions, including specialized espionage, access facilitation and destructive operations.

Featherweight: Groups with narrower or less consistently documented activity, some relying on support from more established adversaries.

“Iran isn’t as technically sophisticated as China, Russia or North Korea, but what it lacks in sophistication it makes up for in cadence,” said Francis Guibernau, Senior Adversary Research Engineer at AttackIQ. “They target anything and everything, on every operating system and in industrial environments. That volume, combined with how freely these groups share access, is what makes the ecosystem dangerous.”

Related:Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, but Payments Decline

The research draws on more than 200 references and consolidates more than 2,600 procedures, 1,300 file indicators, and 2,300 network indicators. The analysis was also validated against threat intelligence and real-world activity observed by several Fortune 150 companies actively targeted by Iranian threat actors. The research team also received input from National Computer Incident Response Teams (CIRTs) and members of the intelligence community.

To help organizations put the research into practice, AttackIQ will be releasing adversary emulations based on the documented tactics, techniques, and procedures of Iranian threat actors over the coming weeks. These emulations will enable security teams to safely test their defenses against relevant adversary behaviors, identify gaps in detection and prevention, and prioritize improvements based on real-world threat intelligence.

For a closer look at the findings with AttackIQ’s adversary research team, join the December 10 webinar, Breaking Down Iran’s Most Dangerous Cyber Tactics.

AttackIQ is the leader in threat-informed Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM), helping organizations continuously validate defenses, break attack paths, and reduce threat debt through evidence-based security operations.

Through AVA Agentic OS, AttackIQ has introduced the industry’s first agentic operating system purpose-built for CTEM, enabling organizations to execute Continuous Threat Exposure Management autonomously at enterprise scale.

By orchestrating specialized AI agents across threat intelligence, adversary exposure validation, security validation, detection engineering, control optimization, threat debt reduction, and AI security validation, AttackIQ transforms fragmented security activities into continuous cyber resilience.

Trusted by the world’s largest enterprises, government agencies, and managed security providers, AttackIQ empowers organizations to continuously discover, validate, and reduce cyber risk with confidence.

#9805. Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:

No need for torchrun: the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:

Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

#9804. Strike Graph Launches Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool

New agentic AI solution leverages APIs to collect compliance evidence from systems and applies it to over 30 frameworks with no duplicate work.

SEATTLE, November 18, 2026 — Strike Graph, the enterprise AI-native governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) management platform, today announced a new integration solution that seamlessly connects to any software API to automatically collect compliance evidence from it. With Integration AI, organizations using the Strike Graph platform are no longer limited to a fixed integration catalog. They simply indicate the system they are using and Strike Graph builds a native integration that pulls compliance evidence from it automatically.

Once connected via an API, the Strike Graph platform employs an AI research agent to read the vendor’s public API documentation and draft a build specification. Concurrently, a second AI agent builds the complete integration across Strike Graph’s backend, user interface, and evidence pipeline. Integrations connect API-to-API, and customers never install agents or software inside their own infrastructure, which is critical for maintaining enterprise-grade security.

Related:It's a Bot World. We're Just Living in It

“For compliance to be successful, access to evidence must be quick, easy, and continuous, but integration with existing tools often presents a challenge,” said Justin Beals, CEO and founder of Strike Graph. “Integration AI has empowered Strike Graph to overcome those roadblocks and accomplish all three of those requirements at once. If it has an API, Strike Graph can collect evidence from it. Furthermore, since Strike Graph’s evidence model is graph-based, evidence from a newly built integration automatically counts toward every framework a customer pursues, including SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, and CMMC, with no duplicate work.”

As with all Strike Graph evidence collection integrations, Integration AI builds secure integrations that are restricted to read-only operations by default. Each one carries an endpoint allowlist that ratifies against the vendor’s real API documentation, which guarantees evidence collection can observe a customer’s systems but never change or impact them.

Strike Graph keeps strict separation where credentials are never touched by Integration AI.The build process works outside of the core governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) program itself, building the connection with no access to any customer secrets. Credentials and other sensitive data live in a securely managed secrets vault, and the build spec is scanned and automatically rejected if any credentials are detected in it.

With Integration AI, vendor documentation is treated strictly as data and never as instructions, which blocks prompt-injection attempts hidden in third-party content. The AI build environment holds no publishing rights, and a separate locked-down step does the publishing.

Related:Satellites Have a Ground-Level Cybersecurity Problem

Builds sit behind an approver allowlist and a kill switch, and humans are always in the loop to review the research plan before build starts, after code has been written, and before anything is deployed to production. The AI can only propose changes, not ship them, and every integration requires a human engineering review.

Once built, Integration AI runs evidence scripts in self-contained isolated sandbox environments with no shared code paths, so a flaw in one integration can’t spread to another.

Integration AI is available to Strike Graph customers today. For more information, visit www.strikegraph.com.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

InfoQ Homepage News .NET MAUI 11 Makes CoreCLR the Default Runtime and Adds Incremental XAML Hot Reload

Nov 26, 2026 3 min read

Microsoft released .NET 11 on 10 November, and .NET MAUI in .NET 11 changes the default runtime from Mono to CoreCLR on all supported platforms. It also adds incremental XAML hot reload, implicit XAML namespaces and new test project templates. The work spanned seven previews and a release candidate, and the documentation describes product quality as the release's focus.  Overall, this release consolidates more than it expands.

.NET MAUI (Multi-platform App UI) is Microsoft's cross-platform UI framework for Android, iOS, Mac Catalyst and Windows apps built from one C# and XAML codebase. .NET 11 is a Standard Term Support release with two years of support. Microsoft notes that MAUI follows its own support policy, separate from the runtime's STS and LTS lifecycle.

The runtime switch is the most significant change. According to Microsoft, CoreCLR puts mobile and desktop apps on the same runtime as the other .NET workloads. Release builds use composite partial ReadyToRun by default. On Apple platforms, which disallow JIT compilation, code that isn't precompiled runs in the CoreCLR interpreter. Native AOT is an opt-in publishing option, and its Android support is still experimental. Microsoft recommends developers to test app libraries before choosing their deployment model.

XAML gets four main improvements. First, incremental hot reload, still in preview, patches live instances of pages and controls without recreating them. It is on by default in Debug builds, works with dotnet watch, and can be disabled with EnableMauiIncrementalHotReload. Second, implicit namespace declarations are now on by default, so the root xmlns and xmlns:x are optional. Third, lazy ResourceDictionary loading makes large dictionaries initialise up to roughly eight times faster when XAML source generation is used. Finally, RelativeSource bindings with a resolvable AncestorType now compile to trim-safe code.

Handlers keep replacing the legacy renderers with newer implementations. Windows uses the new CollectionView2 handler by default, Android Shell is now handler-based, and iOS and Mac Catalyst now use handlers for NavigationPage, TabbedPage and FlyoutPage. The old renderers remain available as a manual fallback. On iOS, Appearing now fires before a page is pushed rather than after it becomes visible, and secondary toolbar items move into an overflow menu. Developers who depend on the old timing should switch to NavigatedTo.

Controls get smaller additions. Maps gain clustering and custom pin icons, plus an Azure Maps-backed implementation on Windows. TabbedPage gains badges, BoxView a Fill brush, and LongPressGestureRecognizer becomes configurable. Shell also supports route templates such as trip/{tripId}.

Animation methods now accept a CancellationToken, and their non-Async variants are obsolete. On the platform side, a new Passkeys class in Microsoft.Maui.Authentication wraps WebAuthn creation and assertion, while the server still has to validate challenges and attestation. Permissions.PostNotifications now works on iOS, and splash screens can have dark-mode variants.

For Android, the minimum API level rises from 21 to 24, and x86 architecture is no longer supported. The release notes report shorter builds: an incremental build after a managed source change dropped from 68.3 to 52.3 seconds. They also report startup gains of 2.4 to 4.5 per cent from partial ReadyToRun, at the cost of a slightly larger package. Apple targets now require iOS, tvOS and Mac Catalyst 18.2 and macOS 15.2, with Xcode 26.4.

Several changes break existing code. The Microsoft.Maui.Controls.Compatibility package no longer ships, the Color record is now sealed, Java.Lang.Object.JavaFinalize() is obsolete, and non-font SwipeItem icons are no longer tinted automatically. When upgrading, Microsoft advises to focus on throughly testing navigation, custom handlers and trimmed publishing.

The full list of changes, including per-preview release notes, is in the .NET MAUI documentation. .NET MAUI ships as a workload with NuGet packages, so a project can pin specific versions.

#9799. Russia's Cold Relic APT Turns One Cloud Breach Into Another

The state-sponsored threat group is using data stolen from one victim to target others via convincing impersonations and social engineering attacks.

The Russian cyber-espionage group known as Cold Relic is turning cloud breaches into a springboard for targeting a victim organization's wider network of trusted relationships.

It's a tactic that researchers at Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) observed the attacker deploy with clinical efficiency in two separate compromises involving US organizations over the past year.

In the first intrusion, late last year, the attackers gained control of a cloud administrator account and harvested internal communications, employee details, and other organizational records. Cold Relic actors later used that material to impersonate an employee of the first organization for a successful social engineering attack on an individual at a second organization.

The activity, GTIG researchers said, shows how traditional social engineering is becoming more closely tied to attacks on cloud identities. Once inside an organization's cloud environment, an attacker can gather the kind of internal information that makes a message from a supposedly trusted colleague or business contact much harder to spot as a scam.

Related:Cyprus Becomes Espionage Target for Iranian Hackers

The campaigns "demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse," GTIG researchers wrote in a blog post. "By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners."

Cold Relic (also known as Star Blizzard, Callisto, and Gossamer Bear) is a cyber-espionage group that Google researchers have been tracking — and disrupting — since 2015. The US government has assessed the outfit as working within Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) and tasked with collecting information of political and strategic interest to Moscow.

Though low-profile, Cold Relic has notched up numerous high-value targets including defense contractors, government officials, and NGOs across North America and Europe. One of its favorite post-compromise activities, according to GTIG, is to steal emails and data that can help it establish "authentic pretexts" and convincing impersonations when reaching out to other potential targets.

In the first intrusion in late 2025, Cold Relic used stolen credentials for a super admin account to access a US organization's cloud environment. The attackers routed their activity through a residential proxy located near the organization, so their connections appeared to originate from a familiar geographic area. The attacker repeatedly kept sending the actual account holder multifactor authentication (MFA) push notifications until the overwhelmed user approved one.

Related:Latin America Sees Cyberattacks on Ports, Pipelines & Manufacturing

After gaining access, Cold Relic actors registered their own device on the network and established additional ways to authenticate to it, including via passkeys, backup MFA codes, and additional rogue MFA devices. The threat group used the stolen Super Admin user privileges to exfiltrate the organization's cloud storage, including full employee lists, email conversations, and organizational directories and contact lists. The threat actors then initiated several anti-forensics measures that allowed it to maintain access to the compromised network for several months.

In the second attack, earlier this year, Cold Relic impersonated an employee of the first company to contact an individual at a second organization through an encrypted messaging app. The threat actors sent the unsuspecting target phishing links disguised as documents relevant to their ongoing conversation.

After stealing the victim's Microsoft Entra ID credentials and authentication tokens, Cold Relic used them to access the organization's Google Workspace environment through its federated single sign-on system. The attackers then helped themselves to files from the compromised user's cloud drive while also seeking out email archives, chat records, credentials, personnel information, and other data of potential intelligence value.

Related:AI Agents Zip From Flaw Discovery to Root Access in 11 Minutes

"Cold Relic is highly adept at leveraging social networks and impersonation of key individuals to achieve a realistic pretense for reaching out to the targeted individual or organization," Wes Shields, security engineer at GTIG, tells Dark Reading. "Once they have achieved their initial access goal, they move quickly to maintain persistence and exfiltrate data."

The lesson for organizations is to train employees to be wary of unexpected messages, particularly when they arrive through communication channels a supposed colleague or business contact doesn't normally use. If a message seems unusual, employees should verify the sender's identity through a separate, previously established channel before responding or acting on it, Shields advises.

"In today's hyper-connected world, it is impossible to have employees not be reachable via multiple channels, and attackers are taking advantage of this," he says.

Joseph Spero, principal incident response consultant at Google, recommends other measures to limit the damage from identity-based attacks. These include enforcing phishing-resistant MFA, restricting and auditing passkey registrations, hardening MFA registration procedures, and auditing OAuth grants.

"Short-lived sessions and the principle of least privilege will limit the potential scope of access when credentials are compromised," he says. "When a compromise is suspected, mandate session revocation in addition to resetting passwords and MFA mechanisms."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9797. Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:

The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:

Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

#9796. Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Nigeria faced more than double the cyber threats of the previous year, with Angola and Kenya also in the top 5 most-attacked countries globally.

Organizations in Africa faced an average of 3,834 cyberattacks per week in October, a jump of 38% from a year earlier, making the continent the most-attacked region for the first time in more than a year.

Nigeria, Angola, and Kenya were among the top-five most targeted countries, with Nigeria topping the list with nearly 6,700 attacks targeting organizations in the country every week; that marks a 140% increase over October 2025, according to data published by Check Point Research earlier this month. The nations are among those rapidly pushing technological transformation of their infrastructure, expanding connectivity, investing in digital services, and putting sensitive data in network-connected applications and storage.

The fast transformation is exposing more opportunities for attackers, says Shayimamba Conco, chief technology officer and security evangelist in the Office of the CTO at Check Point Software.

Related:Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry

"All this rapid digital expansion is now happening within the region, but then, at the same time, this [expansion] is outpacing improvements in security maturity," he says, adding that security improvements are uneven across the continent. "Yes, some areas — let's say for example, South Africa — it's adopting cybersecurity at a much quicker rate than the rest of the Africa region, but there will be those regions which are still lagging behind a bit."

The significant increase in average weekly attacks pushed African organizations past those in Latin America as the favored targets of cyberattackers. In the first quarter of 2026, Latin America averaged more than 3,000 attacks per week, surpassing the approximate 2,700 attacks targeting African organizations. In September, the two regions essentially tied in terms of attacks, with Africa once again becoming the most popular target in October.

Globally, organizations experienced an average of 2,550 weekly cyberattacks in October, down 9% from September but up a third from the previous year. While Africa encountered the most weekly attacks, both Latin America and Asia-Pacific regions saw a greater-than-average number — 3,483 and 3,436, respectively.

Globally, cyberattacks focused heavily on the education sector, with the average academic institution suffering more than 5,900 attacks per week, up a third from the same month in 2025. The education sector has topped the global list of popular targets every month, with organizations made attractive to attackers because of their large data sets and reliance on legacy systems, says Conco.

Related:Malicious Linux Implants Mimic Asian Mail Security Products

"There is a lack of budget when it comes to not just IT, but specifically cybersecurity," he says. "A junior IT engineer has to manage these vast environments, which are hard to lock down by nature, because you've got all these students who need access to all these applications and resources."

In Africa, however, cyberattackers most often targeted financial services, government agencies, and the energy sector, according to Check Point's data.

The countries are racing to improve their cybersecurity postures and address persistent threats. Nigeria's National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) continues to work on the details of the nation's cybersecurity and cloud-sovereignty policies. Last month, Operation Serengeti 3.0 — a joint task force between Interpol and 20 African countries — led to the arrest of more than 1,500 suspects and the recovery of $105 million in stolen funds. In August, Operation Jackal IV targeted West African crime syndicates, leading to more than 200 arrests.

Check Point also flagged the use of AI in companies as a potential weak point, finding that about 2.9% of prompts to generative AI and large language models (LLMs) posed a high risk of leaking sensitive information. The risk is steadily increasing over time, from 2.3% in August to 2.5% in September.

Related:UAE, Saudi Arabia Face Onslaught of Increasingly Complex Cyberattacks

Interpol has also observed that attackers are increasingly using AI in a way that has impacted African nations. In its African Cybercrime Assessment Report 2026, Interpol found that 55% of reported cybercrimes across Africa used AI to some degree.

"Cybercrime has emerged as one of the most significant criminal threats to the region," Neal Jetton, Director of Interpol’s Cybercrime unit, said in a statement in August. "AI is automating every stage of a cyberattack from reconnaissance and phishing to extortion and evasion. However, we see that when countries work together, cybercriminal infrastructure can be identified, disrupted and dismantled."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).
