InfoQ Homepage Presentations Finetuning Your Embedding Model for Better Search: Learning from Agentic Search at Dell

Rachel Shalom explains how Dell solved enterprise RAG retrieval failures on internal terminology by fine-tuning open-source embedding models. She discusses data prep with hard negatives, distributed InfoNCE loss training on H100 GPUs, automated hyperparameter tuning, and production evaluation using LLM-as-a-judge.

Rachel Shalom is an applied AI scientist and Distinguished Engineer with 7+ years of experience turning cutting edge AI into real world impact. She specializes in LLM-based knowledge retrieval, multi-agent systems, and deep learning for time series data, building solutions that don’t just work, they get used.

QCon AI is a practitioner-led event focused entirely on the engineering discipline required to scale these workloads safely. It provides direct access to the architectural playbooks and failure metrics that peer organizations use in production.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

Rachel Shalom: I'm Rachel. I work for Dell. I'm part of a team that develops internal AI solutions for Dell. We develop solutions that basically Dell employees are using. I'm going to talk about some of the work we are doing inside Dell today. I'm actually going to start with the motivation of this talk. I'm leading an agentic search within Dell, a search system that searches for your information in internal sources like GitHub, Jira, Confluence, and other sources. Part of it is using semantic search, which is using also an embedding model. What we have noticed is that we keep failing in certain type of questions. Questions that have to do with internal terminology or questions that have to do with internal products of Dell. Here are some examples like PowerScale or CloudIQ or PowerProtect. These are the type of questions that are using internal terminology, or you can call it even internal language of Dell, that the system kept failing with retrieving the right answer. The motivation was, does the embedding model that is supposed to capture the meaning of those really understand the questions or the answers?

This is what we are going to talk about today. We'll discuss why embedding models are important and common training methodologies. We'll discuss also the common use cases for embeddings. I will talk about fine-tuning and a common loss function that is used today for training majority of the embedding models. We will talk about the use case at Dell more in depth and why we trained our own embedding model, discuss the data collection, and how did we evaluate and monitor the performance.

Humans understand words, machines understand numbers. Embeddings is the bridge between them. Embedding is capturing the meaning of words and sentences. For example, you can see in that lane that in the embedding space, expressions that have to do with password or forgot my login or can't access account should be closer in the embedding space, while cities and countries will be in a different area in the embedding space, but closer to each other, and that's the meaning of representations. What are the common use cases for using embedding models? I think the most common one is information retrieval. Most of the companies or at least in the enterprise, you use RAG, Retrieval-Augmented Generation to retrieve information from a vector database. Classification is one more. For example, if you want to assign categories to your text, like you have incoming emails, the most trivial example is you want to target spam or not spam. Clustering is another very common use case for embedding models. If you want to make sense of your unstructured data, like you have incoming queries by customers and you want to group them together into clusters and recommendation systems to make personalized recommendations. There are probably others, but these are the most common ones.

Now I want to talk briefly on the general training procedures for embedding models. Usually when you train embedding models, you start with the first phase, which is the pre-training. Pre-training is done on what we call the chunk of the internet. You take everything that is available online, Wikipedia, books, public GitHub repository, anything you can imagine, and it's a lot of data, and it can be also junk data, but it's a lot of data that you put in. The way you train is by Masked Language Modeling, which means, as you see in the example, is that you give the model a sentence, each time you mask a different word, and then you let the model guess the word, and this is how you teach the model a general understanding of the language. A little bit of grammar, a little bit of word connections, but a very general understanding, not the fine-grained understanding of semantic meaning of each word, and for that, you have stage number two, which is a fine-tuning stage.

At this stage, you really have to collect high-quality data. Usually it takes a long time, and it costs a lot of money normally. I'm going to talk about the preparation of what we call contrastive learning, which is a very common way to train or fine-tune embedding models nowadays. What you do normally is you prepare pairs or triplets of examples. For example, here, you have a question. Let's call it an anchor. How do I reset my password? Then you have a positive answer, which is how to reset it, and then you have a negative answer, which doesn't answer your question. The idea in training is that you want to teach the model that the question and the positive answer will be represented as vectors that are very close in the embedding space, and the negative answer and the anchor are going to be further apart. That's the goal of the fine-tuning, to take high-quality data and get the real semantic meaning for the text.

How do you do that? I'm putting here a little bit of mathematics, and I'm going to explain each part of it. I think it's beautiful, and this is important that you will see it. InfoNCE, or the long-term in parentheses, loss function is one of the most common ones. If you take a look at different papers from Google or anyone else that is training embedding models, you will see different versions of the same loss function, but this is the basic one. If we go and see the batch, or we have let's say 100 examples of questions and answers, so if we take a look at a log expression, you will see that on the top we have the exponent of s is a cosine similarity between two vectors, the vector of the question and the vector of the positive answer. On the denominator, you're going to see again the similarity of the question and the positives, and the similarity of the question and negatives.

All other documents that are not the positive one to this question are considered negatives, because they are not directly answering the question. When you train an embedding model, the purpose is to bring up the similarity for positives and bring down the similarity for negatives. I added another slide for that just to maybe show it in a geometric way, so that you don't lose the context. Again, we have this log loss of positives versus negatives. If we take a look at the lower part, then you can see that if I have, let's say, a query, how do I reset my password? Then I have a positive question and a bunch of negative questions. Then, before training, you will see that the distance between the positive and negative vectors to the query are maybe, let's say, a little bit similar, and after training, you want to see that the positive answer is closer to the query, and the negatives are further away. I hope you at least enjoyed a little bit from this loss function. It's super beautiful.

Another thing that is interesting about the training is what we call prefix use. What does that mean? Sometimes we have what we call conflicting reward signals. Think about a model that is performing different tasks. Sometimes it is questions and answers. Sometimes it is clustering, as we mentioned before. Sometimes it is other tasks. Then if we take a look at this example, what is the capital of France? I want you to answer what is mostly similar, answer number one or answer number two. I think the answer would be it depends on the task. If we want to do clustering similarity between two sentences, then what is the capital of France, and number one would be more similar. If my task is to pair questions and answers, then what is the capital of France, and number two is more similar. In order to solve that, what is commonly done today when training with fine-tuning is to add prefixes.

As you can see, we have in orange the start clustering, what is the capital of France, and then clustering the answer, and that tells the model, please create vectors for clustering. They're going to get slightly different vectors because the task now is to say, these are two similar sentences. If I provide a different prefix, which is search_query, search_document, so the task is questions and answers. This is where you give the model a signal that we are now talking about a different task. This is one important thing to notice when training.

I've talked a little bit about the use cases and a little bit generally about the training. Now let's talk about Dell, or what we did at Dell. We have an agentic search at Dell, which means we let R&D teams search within all of Dell's internal sources. For example, Jira, Confluence, GitHub, these are mostly relevant for engineers and product managers, SharePoint, also different databases. I'm going to talk about the architecture, but this is a hierarchical architecture of multiple agents that are making API calls. It also has a component of semantic search, which means we take all the data and ingest it in advance. It has a component of memory management, which is pretty common for agentic search applications. It's also permission aware, which is very important for any enterprise. These are some of the questions that we are getting normally, questions about bug solving, questions about onboarding to a new project, testing, technical configurations, procedural how-to.

We get all sorts of also weird questions, but these are the most common ones. This is a little bit on the architecture of the system itself. We have the orchestrator, or what we call the supervisor, which is the entry point for every question. This is a router that routes the user question to any other of the agents. We have a GitHub agent, which means that it's a model with a set of tools, mainly API tools. We have a Confluence agent that is a model. They all have access, or it's access-based, to the information inside Dell. We have GitLab and GitHub, which is, again, exactly the same. Models with different API tools. We have security agent, which usually makes API calls to OSs like Ubuntu and SUSE, and provide CVE resolutions, and agents that are making database queries. Just to note that each one of these agents are talking only to the supervisor.

We keep them that way in order to keep the context low and the context in place. We found it more effective that way. The supervisors can route the question to one or many agents. They return back an answer. The supervisor decides, do I want to go back to the user with an answer, or go back to the agents and bring another one? We, of course, limit the number of turns, so it won't take like one hour to get back to the user. This is how it works.

That is when someone wants to create their own bot, let's say, you just provide, here is a link to my Confluence or to my Jira, to my GitHub, and then it triggers a pipeline that does a lot of data plumbing, and ingest and chunk all the data, put it in a vector database, and it's ready for you to query. You can create your personal context space. A little bit more about the bring your own data architecture, it's important because this is the part that connects later to our embedding model, which is the main subject. If you have Jira, Confluence, and GitHub, we're taking all of the fields from Confluence, we take all the images and attachments, and so is for Jira. We do semantic chunks with code. We use AST, and we do a lot of cleanups, like these are too many details to talk about.

Then you might ask yourself, ok, so you do all of that job, but the rate of change is very high, so we update it every two days. We go and check with the APIs what were the changes, and then we re-embed all the changes every two days. Everything is saved in pgvector, which is, again, hosted on-prem, which I think is very nice that everything is hosted on-prem at Dell, that it's all private, nothing goes out. Just a little bit about chunking. I'm talking only on Confluence now because the work that we did in training the model, the context was Confluence. We start with an API fetch, or think about Confluence space, if you work with Confluence, you download thousands of pages, then we reformat it into HTML. We filter a lot of noise because there are a lot of emojis and stuff that are not relevant to the model, we turn it into an md file. We detect also tables to make sure that the context of the table is saved even when you chunk. We take all those attachments and then we chunk by paragraphs and use an embedding model and save it in a vector database. This is done for every request that we get and in advance.

Now the question is, ok, so we have a system in place, we have lots of agents and we have also semantic search, now why fine-tune our own embedding? I started the lecture with saying that we saw gaps that the semantic search just didn't solve, and the gaps were mainly about questions on internal products, on abbreviations and acronyms that are specific to Dell, and workflows and processes, everything that is the Dell world or the Dell language, there are a lot of such data at Dell, that led us to think or to hypothesize that this is a reason for failure. Now when you run a RAG system, so there are potentially a lot of problems that could happen. It has a lot of stages and a lot of pieces moving around, so it could be something else. Our hypothesis said, let's try and see if we can improve the result by fine-tuning a model.

Generally speaking, I think that the signals you want to look for if you are planning a domain adaptation are to ask yourself like, is the data of the model out of the shelf that I'm taking on? Now I'm talking about models in the context of open source. We take most of the models from Hugging Face, normally you know what is the training data that they were trained on, you have leaderboards. You ask yourself, is the Dell data even similar to what those models were trained on? It can be that the terminology we use was used when this model was trained originally. These are the signs to look for when you want to train. There is another interesting thing to check. Again, every open-source model comes with a vocabulary. It's a list of tokens that the model has seen. This one was around 30,000. What happens when the model hasn't seen that word, they have a special token called unknown token.

That means the model said, I haven't seen that but I can manage, never mind. I put an unknown token. I wanted to understand how many unknown tokens do we have that the model completely hasn't seen at all? Not that it doesn't understand the semantics, it just didn't see those words. I was surprised to see that these are very general. I put here some examples that I saw, like Base64-encoded strings, or you can see Unicode box-drawing, all of these things that really have no meaning. It makes sense. All of the images, the model didn't recognize, that was surprising. I thought that models are trained on images now. Checkmarks and long camelCase compound words. This was a very small percentage of the data that the model didn't recognize. The reason I checked it is because when you fine-tune a model, I would like the model to semantically understand my data. If most of the tokens that I have in my data do not exist in the model vocabulary, that's a reason to start training from scratch, not fine-tuning. That was a check. The check told me, it's fine. The model doesn't understand images. I don't care. Let's move on. We are continuing with fine-tuning.

There is also the inference cost and latency. How fast is this model? Does it support multilingual and not only English? Lastly, the context length. How much text can I push in at once? Then we ended up at comparing two, EmbeddingGemma and Nomic Embed, mainly because we were very limited in the licensing part. Just a funny story, before we used those, we used the BGE family. These are Chinese family. Then for some reason, Chinese models were banned from some American companies. Then we had to redo the whole work with models that are allowed. Both of them have great licenses. They are both open, even though I must say that comparing to Google, Nomic Embed by Nomic, they released it all. You are welcome to go and try. They released the training code, the model, the data. Anyone can reproduce the work. It's amazing. In terms of parameters or size, both of them are tiny, so it's great.

They are really fast. Context length, you can see that Google contains only 2K and Nomic Embed contains 8K. Google supports multilingual. If I go to best fit, then we decided, I have a choice now between Confluence, GitHub, and Jira. Now when we took a look at Google, they were very optimized for code search. We chose the EmbeddingGemma for code embedding. For Confluence, we decided we go with Nomic Embed because it has extensive technical documents it was trained on. Also, the context length gives us more flexibility when we want to embed things from Confluence.

Going back to Confluence, I want to talk a little bit about, we decided now to fine-tune, now how do you start. You need to start preparing data, that's the hardest part, harder than just fine-tuning. We started with taking chunks, and I'm going to provide examples in the next slide. The chunking part, we did already in advance, so it was easy just to take the chunks we already handled. Then, step two, once I have one chunk, let's say, I'm taking an LLM to help me generate questions for that chunk. We generated three questions for each chunk, and of course, you can play with the number, that the chunks are supposed to answer those questions. This is how you generate, as you remember, the question and the positive document. Now, I would like to generate the negative documents. How do I do that? I have the questions, so we did a trick, and we took each question, and we went to the vector database, and we say, ok, let's take a model that wasn't trained, and retrieve documents from our vector database, but just, let's cap it so that the similarity when we retrieve is larger than 30%, but less than 80%.

We keep it in a range where the answer probably is not the most exact answer, but are not very far away. It's what we call hard negatives. They are answers that are not exactly answering what you ask, but they're not very far away, and we want to distinguish between those. We took the top 20, once you have 20 for the training, we kept 7 out of them. The number of negatives per training is just a parameter, and you can decide what to do. Then, you create triplets out of this process. How do you create triplets? That was a description of the process, so it's important you see one example in front of you, so a passage. We have to install Windsurf on Ubuntu WSL, just install. This is a chunk that we have. Now, I need to generate three questions out of it with an LLM.

As you can see, I generated three questions that are in purple, and the answers in green are exactly this identical chunk. Now, I went to the database and I retrieved other chunks that are going to be the negative answers. In this process, I've created to myself three samples. Each sample contains one question, one answer, and one document that is positive documents, and then seven negative documents.

I wanted to take a look at the data to see and check two things. On the top, I wanted to check the number of tokens for each part. I wanted to see what is the distribution of tokens for the questions, and you see it's roughly between zero to 50. This is a sample. Then I wanted to see what is the token distribution for the positive answers, which are roughly up to 1,500. Then I wanted to see what is the distribution of the negative answer, which are the same, up to 1,000, but we add a little bit more. This is important because the model is limited by context, so you want to make sure that you don't have very large context. Second thing is the cosine similarity distribution. As you see below, I wanted to compare the distribution of the question and the positives, and the question of the negatives.

What would you expect it to be? In a perfect world, I would expect that the distribution of question and the positive document would be very high, and take it to the right, the green one should be on the right. The distribution of similarities between negatives and the question would be to the left, very low similarities. As you can see here, it's a start where they are pretty similar. My goal, or what I will check after I'm going to train, is if I manage to create that separation, meaning the similarities of positives are going to be on the right side, and similarities of negatives are going to be on the left side. One more thing about fine-tuning with Auto Research. Some of you have trained models in the past. You know that, at least in the past, it was babysitting the models. You have a lot of parameters to play with in the model, learning rate, batch size, whatever it is.

Every time, you do a round, you wait a few hours, and then you start with different parameters. I think a month ago, Andrej Karpathy released what they called Auto Research, and he said, I just created an md file. I told the model, it's an LLM training an LLM. That's what it is. I gave my Claude Code, I think it was Opus 4.6. I told it, here is a training loop, here is the configuration file. You are only allowed to play with the training code and the parameters and the configuration, nothing else. Don't stop until the human stops you. Just make experiments. Each experiment should last 10 minutes, and then check the loss. If the loss goes down, keep those parameters. Loss goes up, remove those parameters, and move on. I just let it run overnight, and it really did save me a lot of time, because I came up, I looked at the experiment he made. I must say that there were some stupid stuff he did, but I chose one of the experiments that I liked, and I set up the learning rate, and the batch size, and everything, to what just the model told me. It was a nice experiment, and I think it is saving time.

I wanted to tell you a little bit about the setup for training. First of all is, I ran on four H100 GPUs. After all, I work at Dell, they have a lot of infrastructure. The number of negatives is 7. I used batch size of 128, and remember, the training data was Confluence spaces of almost all Dell. I counted the tokens, it was around 9 billion tokens in total. Then I wanted just for us to talk, or have a pick on distributed training. Let's take a look at the first part. If I have four GPUs, and I say I have 128 batch size, what does it mean in terms of documents? It means that I have 128 queries, or questions, and then I have, for each one of them, one positive answer, seven negative answers. I ended up with 1,024 additional documents on each GPU. Each GPU is getting one model, and 1,024 documents plus 128 queries.

We go to stage two. We start with the forward path. We put in the text, and we get vectors. What is interesting with this forward path is that, first, it is done in batches. It is done in batches of 32 in order to minimize memory consumption, but also, it is done in a way, we don't save any gradients, or the computational graph, let's call it. If you use PyTorch, so when saving a computational graph, it means you save the whole million parameters model activations, and it takes a lot of memory. When you don't save it, reduces the memory. What do you end up with after you do the forward path? You end up with vector. You started with text, now you have vector. Each vector is a dimension of 768. If we have 128 questions, so only for those, you end up with a matrix of 128 over the dimension of the vector, 768.

This is only for the queries. What else do we have? We have all the documents. We have 1,024 documents that are converted now to vectors in the size dimension of 768. What happened next? You have the all-gather. Each GPU now is collecting all the information from other GPUs. Now each GPU holds 4,096 vectors in a dimension of 768. Now we want to compute the loss. Remember the loss that we presented in the past where we want to compute similarities between the questions and positive answers and negative answers. This is where it is done. What is interesting here is that each GPU is seeing one question, one positive answer, and all the rest are going to be the negatives. You are getting now 4,095 negatives to compare against one positive. Why is it good? Because this is a harder task when the model is training. If you manage to train the model well, this is going to be a high-quality model because the task was differentiating between one question and 4,095 negative answers. Eventually when we do loss backward, there is the GradCache and surrogate trick to reduce memory when you calculate gradients. After we calculate the gradients on each GPU, you average them and then you update the model weights and start all over again.

This was a little bit about the distributed training at a high level. Now I want to go back to my EDA before on similarities. Remember that we said that we have similarities, the green one is the similarities between positives and questions, red is negative and questions. I wanted to say that I want to separate between them. You see the distribution before training and after training. As you can see, after training, you can see better separation, which means that it gives me a good signal or it gives me a signal, ok, the training did something well. Because now I see a separation, I see that the similarities of the questions and positive answers are a little bit more to the right. The question and the negative answer are a little bit more to the left. Yes, it's not perfect, there is still an overlap, but it's better than what it was.

Said, ok, good signal, let's continue. What do we need to check now? Let's talk about the evaluation setup. We have gathered what we call a golden dataset of 300 SME-verified questions, answers, and sources. Sources are like, if I ask you, how do I get Windsurf access? Then you will get an answer, but you will also get the links for Confluence that provide this answer. What I wanted to check is the recall @k, meaning, basically the question is, when I retrieve now, do I have the right sources? Did I retrieve the right URLs or not? When I say recall @1 is when I retrieve from the vector database, then it's top 1. Recall @10, it's top 10, organized by similarity. What we discovered is that, yes, we managed to fetch more correct sources when using the new models. I checked, let's say, top one or top five, but in reality, when you do a search system, you don't take top three or top five.

You take like more top 20. This is just for comparison to understand, ok, did I manage to get more or did I not? It seems like I did manage, at least in 12%, to get more resources right. Then, what is more interesting is eventually we are talking about a system that will provide eventually an answer to the user. What I care about is, did we provide the right answer? We did it, again, on the benchmarks that we built, using LLM-as-a-judge. LLM-as-a-judge has different aspects. One of them is question to answer. I want to know, does the text directly address the question? A2A is answer to answer, meaning does the answer match the ground truth? Because I have the ground truth. Here we saw an increase of a little bit more than 4%. It seems like, I would call it a good improvement, yes? Not a great success, but a very good improvement.

We said, ok, let's deploy it. What do you do in order to monitor? You would fine-tune your model. You have now a new model, and you want to say, do I need to retrain? What do I do? The first thing we do is we check the rate of data change. If we are talking about Confluence, we can check within a month, how much did it change? Do we have 1 million new pages? This is already a reason to start retraining. Check for data drift. You can check the distribution of the training data and compare it to your production data. The last thing is we actually have signs from our systems. If people are using our web application, they have the ability to put thumbs up and thumbs down. Also, we check if they click on the actual sources we provide on the website. If they stop clicking, it gives us a bad sign.

I hope that you will take away the importance of embedding. I think it's a topic that is normally overlooked. People are talking about embedding, but they don't understand how beautiful it is. Also wanted to talk a little bit about when fine-tuning is needed, a peek into the data preparation we did there and how we train, and why is it important to monitor and evaluate.

#9792. Why Holiday Security Can't Wait for Black Friday

Bot-driven fraud and holiday social engineering attacks stretch across many weeks, straining security teams and small businesses alike.

Cyber experts have long drawn connections between the accelerated volumes of holiday shopping and threat actors looking for opportunities to take advantage, but as the festive season kicks off, it's important to remember that security posture during this time period is a marathon — not a sprint.

Verizon today published survey results for its holiday trends report, tracking the insights of 600 small business owners and decision-makers in the US. Of those surveyed, 11% said they have dealt with a cyberattack or data-security incident during the holidays, and a third expect to increase cybersecurity investments this holiday season compared with last year.

Meanwhile, managed security services firm VikingCloud this week published a report surveying security and IT leaders which made even steeper claims: a full 86% of respondents said their business has faced at least one successful cyberattack in the past 12 months, and a whopping 98% said at least one came during the 2025 holiday season. And the Retail & Hospitality Information Sharing and Analysis Center (RH-ISAC) last year said the holiday season continues to be the most active fraud environment from a defender standpoint.

Related:Cyber Insurers See New Divide: AI Defense 'Haves' & 'Have Nots'

Some reasons behind the prominence of cyberattacks during this time period are straightforward: Many cybersecurity teams experience lighter staffing during holiday periods and weekends (leaving the door open for easier ransomware attacks). The chaos of the holiday season also means online services and retailers are inundated with activity, giving threat actors cover. And on the social engineering front, the holidays give plenty of pretext for threat actors conducting phishing campaigns (fake emails promising unbelievable Black Friday deals, charity scams, and so on).

Some teams may take this as a cue to prepare for a few select days or weeks of this last part of the year, such as Black Friday or the week leading up to Christmas. But new research around one narrow corner of the threat landscape suggests that may not be wise.

One of the less-discussed types of threat activity retailers face each season is an influx of malicious bots.

F5 today published a study dedicated to automated threat activity leading up to Black Friday. The report analyzed bot and automation traffic across three Black Friday shopping seasons (2023 to 2025) using data from F5 Distributed Cloud Bot Defense. It covers retailers in three retail sub-industries: fashion, e-commerce, and quick-service restaurants (QSR). The report's authors observed that overall automation rose across the three seasons, from 17.4% of transactions in 2023 to 18.5% in 2024, and then 28.6% in 2025.

Related:How Southeastern University Got a Handle on Its Data

The types of activity differ across industries, but F5 observed bots being used for product scraping and inventory hoarding, credential stuffing and account takeover, fake account creation (to claim new user offers), and gift card cracking (inserting gift card numbers into balance checkers to test for valid accounts).

In terms of trends overall, cyberattackers are increasingly leaning toward Web stores over mobile APIs, and a broad rise in bot sophistication over time. But one of the most notable conclusions that F5 researchers made is that there's no single best date to defend. Attackers start their bot onslaught weeks before Black Friday, and continue it well into the weeks after.

As Sean Murphy, F5's field chief information security officer (CISO) for North America, tells Dark Reading, "The data shows that automated activity can be elevated well before the shopping weekend, and the busiest day for automation varied dramatically from year to year."

Bot traffic does not necessarily reflect all threat activity, but there may be a broader lesson here: that steeling your security hygiene for the holiday season is not a few single days or weekends to prepare for but a broader stretch of time that spans from early November to the end of the year. Murphy says security teams "should have monitoring and protections in place throughout the shopping season rather than scaling them up only for Thanksgiving week."

Related:US Cyber Director Pick Signals Shift Toward Expertise

For those in ecommerce dealing with Web and mobile APIs, he urges ensuring protection isn't substantially weaker on one than the other.

"Web traffic had much higher automation rates among the retailers studied, but the report specifically cautions against interpreting that as evidence that APIs are inherently safer. Where API protection is weaker, attackers can shift toward that channel," he says. "And because the dataset contains both simple scripts and automation designed to imitate legitimate users, defenses need to account for a spectrum of bot sophistication rather than relying on a single detection technique."

Finally, he recommends organizations prioritize targeted employee security awareness and training, particularly for those teams handling customer accounts, payments, and other sensitive information. "Many attacks still begin with social engineering and credential theft, so employees need to know how to recognize suspicious requests and protect account access."

Chris Flood, senior vice president and CRO of Verizon Business, tells Dark Reading that small businesses can reduce their risk with four fairly simple steps: require multifactor authentication, train employees how to spot scams, keep guest Wi-Fi separate from payment systems, and keep software and devices updated.

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#9790. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

#9788. Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

This installment of the Reporters' Notebook video series examines the fallout from recent high-severity flaw disclosures, exploring how fears of AI-assisted exploits trigger widespread panic, operational disruptions, and growing warning fatigue.

The pressure on cybersecurity teams to patch critical vulnerabilities is reaching a boiling point, exacerbated by incessant coverage and rapid-fire disclosures of AI-discovered bugs. Last month it was PHP2Shell. This week it's Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a 9.2 CVSS flaw in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder unearthed in just one hour using OpenAI's Codex by Calif Research, and NGINX2Root (CVE-2026-123007), a 9.2 CVSS critical integer underflow vulnerability affecting nginx HTTP/2 discovered by Rapid7 MDR.

In the latest installment of the monthly Reporters' Notebook video series, TechTarget Cybersecurity's Alissa Irei, Cybersecurity Dive's David Jones, and Dark Reading's Fahmida Y. Rashid discussthe PHP2Shell vulnerability and examine whether the industry is falling victim to communal panic.

PHP2Shell refers to two critical PHP vulnerabilities — CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 — discovered by Calif (the same company that found Java4Shell) and rated 9.2 on the CVSS scale. Caused by out-of-memory corruption and stale global state errors, the flaws enable unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on Web servers without requiring credentials or prior access. Following a rocky, coordinated disclosure process marked by accidental leaks on X, many organizations preemptively pulled websites and critical services offline, fearing that threat actors leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) would rapidly launch automated attacks before Web servers and applications could be patched.

Related:NIST Enrichment Reductions Impact CVE Coverage, Accuracy

However, the anticipated wave of machine-speed exploits failed to immediately materialize during "Black October," raising questions about whether extreme preemptive shutdowns do more harm than good. While AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, complex exploit paths, hardware dependencies, and flawed proof-of-concept code mean that severe flaws do not automatically lead to immediate compromises, even when attackers use AI. Constantly shuttering operations or broadcasting catastrophes can create early-warning fatigue, akin to ignored national weather alerts, leaving organizations numb when a genuine emergency strikes.

A similar wave of urgency surrounds Java4Shell, where researchers demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution in widely deployed enterprise tools like Keycloak and Jenkins, prompting CISA to call for immediate patching. However, Java4Shell does not have a universal exploit, meaning attackers must consider each application's memory layout and timing, how Base64 is used, and take application-dependent steps to exploit it.

Related:'God Mode' Flaws Could Wreak Border-Control Havoc

A CISO's primary responsibility is not to unilaterally order costly operational shutdowns or carry sole accountability for business risk, but to clearly communicate technical and operational risks to executive leadership equipped to weigh security threats against business continuity. Staying calm, focusing on risk-based prioritization, and adhering to core security fundamentals remain the most effective defenses against modern threats.

Learn more in the video, and also check out other Reporters' Notebook episodes, available here, for insights and coverage from across Informa TechTarget's network of cybersecurity sister sites.

This transcript has been edited for clarity, readability, and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant and human editors. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Hi, and welcome to this month's installment of Reporters' Notebook, featuring reporters from Dark Reading, TechTarget Cybersecurity, and Cybersecurity Dive. I'm Fahmida Rashid, editor-in-chief of Dark Reading. This month, we are going to be talking about scary security vulnerabilities and the lessons we should take about how they're disclosed. So, joining me are Alyssa and Dave.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

Why don't you introduce yourself quickly before we start the topic?

TechTarget Cybersecurity's Alissa Irei: Sure. I'm Alissa Irei, senior reporter with TechTarget, covering cybersecurity news.

Cybersecurity Dive's David Jones: David Jones. I'm a reporter at Cybersecurity Dive

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: All right, let's get started. We had what researchers have been calling PHP2Shell, which were essentially two security vulnerabilities found in some versions of PHP. In some software, using PHP is pretty serious. We're talking memory corruption, the ability to run code on a Web server without logging in.NNNNNNNNNN

We know it was serious and pretty scary because, on the CVSS score, it was a 9.2 out of 10. That's pretty big news. And whenever you tell anyone that by exploiting vulnerabilities, an attacker will be able to run their code on the Web server without logging in, it gets people worried. I believe the patches were out. There was a whole coordinated disclosure.

TTC's Alissa Irei: This struck me as a pretty big deal. Our colleague James Walker wrote a couple of articles on the vulnerabilities themselves and also the disclosure process, which I believe got a little bit rocky in terms of accidental early disclosures on X, and then there was a lot of racing to patch and companies taking their websites down. But yeah, PHP is in use, in, I think, 70% of the world's websites.

Anything that enables remote code execution seems like a really big deal to me. So, I thought it was noteworthy. I know, Dave, your take seems to be a little bit "this meeting could have been an email." Maybe when all is said and done, it was somewhat overblown.

CD's David Jones: I thought it was absolute chaos. I'm still trying to understand exactly what happened last month because the initial rollout of the patch, the disclosure, as you mentioned, was more than a little rocky and the hype around the entire situation in terms of what was actually at risk. That was kind of a bit of a moving target.

We've had situations in the past where there's a lot of concern that you're going to have what is considered systemic risk on such a global scale that large institutions will not be able to manage that risk in a timely manner. Obviously, there are a couple of factors that kind of played into this.

One was the fact that AI was involved in the discovery. With the fact that malicious actors are able to exploit vulnerabilities faster than they ever have been before. There's a great deal of concern in terms of are you able to address these vulnerabilities in a fast-enough method to get those patched, tested, and verified before malicious actors have a chance to attack them? I think what we saw last month was just a lot of preemptive action where major institutions all over the world were basically preemptively taking their sites offline because they had no way of triaging the potential fallout in time to properly address whether or not they were fully protected.

It's still a bit of a mystery to me exactly what happened, whether there was an initial overreaction, whether there were elements of the exploit that we just didn't understand. There was a lot of bad code in a lot of the proofs of concept, and it just never quite amounted to the emergency that it was set up to be.

Maybe it was a good exercise. But we're still trying to get to the bottom of exactly what took place and how we can avoid some of the exaggerated threat that we saw.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: You brought up two really important things that I want to make sure we dig into. The first one was, there was a bit of a fear that because the adversaries have AI, we don't know how fast they're going to be able to launch an attack. And I think that was the reason for some of this panic … you know, take down the website so that we have time to figure it out.

With Log4j, what was it, three days before we started seeing proofs of concept? And I think there was this sense that we don't have those three days anymore. I think, Dave, you make a really good point that maybe this was a good exercise. Maybe we now know that at least for now, it will not be the same day. We're not going to see an attack the day we see the vulnerability.

TTC's Alissa Irei: Well, the tricky thing about that, though, is can we say that? Because AI can move so quickly, it can also move much more slowly than we anticipate. But is today the day? I do think that there's a big question mark around, you know, sophisticated machine-speed AI-enabled attacks that we're not seeing yet. But also, you don't want to be the organization that is the Wikipedia entry for the big one.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Yes. That's true. But I definitely do think that part of that entire response was driven with we don't know when those attacks were coming. But, Dave, you also noted a second point which I thought was really interesting. That even with AI, the exploit path was a lot more complicated to exploit. I think we've always said in our beat that just because there is a vulnerability, just because there is a way to exploit, does not mean it will automatically be exploited. Sometimes the process to do it is hard, and not all attackers are going to take that harder route. And I think this was an example.

CD's David Jones: I think, you know, in a way it's good that we're thinking about how we respond to these types of things. Maybe we're better prepared, but at the same time, I think we don't want to get into a situation where we're crying wolf ahead of time. And at the end of the day, what actually happened?

Was Black October deserved? I mean, was it really that bad a month? Because I've seen worse.

TTC's Alissa Irei: It's a good point. It reminds me of, you know, national disaster weather warnings. At some point, if you go through enough of them and nothing much happens, people become inclined to ignore them. And at some point, that can be quite dangerous. So, I think it's a fair point.

Do you think that this sort of … I think we used the word hysteria in a previous conversation, communal hysteria, if you will. Do you think that this is specific to the AI age? It has this tendency to overreact. Has it grown in the age of AI and given us our fears about adversarial AI, or do you think that this is a pre-existing tendency that we as an industry have?

CD's David Jones: When you're a security team, particularly a security team with limited resources, you can't respond to every critical flaw or even medium- or high-severity flaw.

Whenever you want to, the resource is not there. You have to prioritize; you have to make decisions about the vulnerabilities that are going to affect the most critical technology.

Can I take the proper steps to either slow this process down or stop it before it gets out of control and I lose control over exactly how my operation continues? Because you have certain businesses where you may be operating in an OT environment where you can't afford to shut down for a certain amount of time. You may be running a hospital; you might be running a factory. You might be running fuel through a pipeline. You can't necessarily afford to be offline for a certain amount of time.

It's a difficult thing. I mean, there are probably a lot of organizations that were basically shut down for a certain amount of time, and they lost money, they lost time, they lost productivity. I don't think we can do that each and every time there's a critical situation.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: That's actually the one thing that occurred to me, when Web people were like, we need to take the site down while we figure things out. And I was like, just a couple of weeks prior, we had people taking down their Citrix boxes because there was a vulnerability and we didn't know what was going on. We don't know what's going on, so turn it off. And to Dave's point, we can't turn everything off. So, it's getting to be a priority, but to also understand when something is so bad that it is a turning-off incident. Because I'm worried that we're kind of moving into this state of turning it off every time, and that's just not practical.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: One thing I want to make sure we get a chance to talk about, and I love that Dave mentioned Log4j, because I think it's one of the biggest concerns. So, with Log4j, as a refresher for everyone, it was a vulnerability in a logging framework used by Java applications. And the challenge was that it's used in all sorts of different applications. And so, you could be like, nope, I looked, but I don't have Log4j, not realizing your suppliers were using it. And I think there was a bit of a worry that this might be the same, where I might not be using it, but I don't know who else is.

Which I think is a very legitimate concern. You need to know not just what you have, what your suppliers have, what your partners have. And I think that was the one aspect of PHP2Shell that kind of got a little obscure. That entire concept of thinking broader and bigger is something that really reminded me with this one that vulnerabilities are not just in your stuff; they're in other people's stuff too.

TTC's Alissa Irei: I think it's a great point. And I do worry about the smaller open source projects that have one or two maintainers, and it seems like everyone is drowning in vulnerabilities these days. And what does that mean for teams that are barely teams, and what does that mean for the software supply chain? I think it's a legitimate worry.

CD's David Jones: I'm not sure that a CISO or a frontline security operations team has the authority to take anything out of service without having a conversation higher up the food chain. I mean, you've got to be in a situation where … let's say there's an emergency, you've got to have people kind of above your pay grade where you have conversations where, yeah, we're not going to be producing food for the next few days, maybe. Or we've got to stop these surgeries if you're in a hospital system. The nuclear plant is not going to be, you know, cooling down for maybe a few hours. You've got to have this thought out in terms of, OK, can you explain to somebody who may not be a trained engineer, who may not be versed in these various systems, why you have to move forward and disrupt the entire business operation for a certain amount of time, because if you let it continue, and let's say somebody gets into your IT environment or your OT environment, and you may not be able to see them.

Are you willing to take that risk? Are you going to be held responsible for taking that risk? And who's going to be the C-suite person or the operational leader whoever makes that call that's going to say, "Yeah, go ahead and pull the plug"?

TTC's Alissa Irei: It's a good reminder that ultimately a CISO's job in some of these cases is communicating risk, not deciding how to manage the risk. Because if I'm a CISO, I wouldn't want to be making that decision about shutting down a hospital or a nuclear power plant. It becomes about being able to quickly and accurately communicate the operational risk to someone who is paid to make those decisions.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: We're increasingly seeing situations where the CISO is the one left holding the bag. So yeah, it's definitely a bigger calculation. To Alyssa's point, communicate it; make sure everyone understands what this means so that it's an informed decision.

TTC's Alissa Irei: Actually, this makes me think of two comments that have come up in recent conversations. One was with an analyst who said the CISO's job is and has always been to manage risk to the best of their ability and then take the blame when things go wrong. And she was very clear that that has not changed in the age of AI; it is the continuation of a pattern.

You know, debatable, but on some days I'm sure that feels true if you're a CISO. Another conversation I had recently was about CISO risk and the need for … I think there's some growing murmurs in the CISO community about the need to push back on the risk that is not actually security's bag to hold and be a little bit more vocal and clear about offloading some of that risk to people who are really better equipped and paid to hold it.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: I think overall it's worth saying that yes, this is serious, yes, this is huge, here's a priority list. But you know what? Maybe it is the time to be a little bit contrarian.

Dave, what would you say is the one lesson you want our listeners, our readers, to be taking away?

CD's David Jones: Well, I guess the question I would have is: Are you prepared and properly set up to address such a situation the next time it happens, because it might happen over Thanksgiving.

Let's agree that AI has the ability to find critical flaws that might take a human team days, weeks, or months to find.

There are state actors and sophisticated criminal actors that can get access to an AI-assisted or automated attack. Find out how to best attack a vulnerability. That could happen within the space of days or hours.

You can't have a team on standby 24/7 all the time responding to every alarm that goes off. It's not cost-effective. It's unrealistic. But to be fair, you have to be prepared to respond to that in some way.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Definitely. Alissa, what would you say yours would be?

TTC's Alissa Irei: Mine is much broader and much less useful.

I think I saw it on a tea towel somewhere, but stay calm and look for signs. I think that's what I'm trying to do. I don't really have a good handle on where this is going next. I don't know that anybody does. So, it seems like that's the best that any security team can do. You know, focus on risk, focus on potential impact and prioritizing actions based on that. And in the meantime, to Dave's point, we'll try to avoid communal hysteria and do what we can do when we can do it, as fast as we can do it, and as smartly as we can do it. And I think that's all anybody can ask because, you know, we've never been here before.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: My thought was kind of similar to yours, that the fundamentals still matter. Know what you're securing, keep an eye on how you're working, you know, keeping an eye on your alerts. Yes, everything is a little new because we're now kind of in this age of, you know, things are being found more complicated, faster, but it's still the fundamentals, right? We need to know what we have so that we can secure it quickly and efficiently communicate it. To Dave's point, let's hope that we don't have these kinds of disastrous months every single month because I don't think we're going to be able to keep up with that volume

So, I'm going to say thank you so much for joining me for this month's Reporters' Notebook. I hope you enjoyed the conversation as much as I did. And see you next month.

#9787. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Email Marketing


1. Why is email marketing important?

Email is the marketing tool that helps you  create a seamless, connected, frictionless buyer journey. More importantly, email marketing allows you to build relationships with prospects, customers, and past customers. It's your chance to speak  to them right in their inbox, at a time that suits them. Along with the right message, email can become one of your most powerful marketing channels.

2. What is benefits of email marketing?

Email marketing is best way for creating long term relationship with your clients, and increasing sales in our company.

Benefits of email marketing for bussiness:
  • Better brand recognition
  • Statistics of what works best
  • More sales
  • Targeted audience
  • More traffic to your products/services/newsletter
  • Build credibility
Most  bussinesses are using email marketing and making tons of money with email marketing.

3. What is the simplest day and time to send my marketing emails?


Again, the answer to this question varies from company to company. And again, testing is the way to find out what works best. Typically, weekends and mornings seem to be  times when multiple emails are opened, but since your audience may have different habits, it's best to experiment and then use your  data to decide.

 4. Which metrics should I be looking at?


The two most important metrics for email marketing are  open rate and click-through rate. If your emails aren't opened, subscribers will never see your full marketing message, and if they open them but don't click through to your site, your emails won't convert.

5. How do I write a decent subject line?


The best subject lines are short and to the point, accurately describing  the content of the email, but also catchy and intriguing, so the reader wants to know more. Once Again, this is the perfect place for  A/B testing, to see what types of subject lines work best with your audience. Your call to action should be clear and  simple. It should be somewhere at the top of your email for those who haven't finished reading the entire email,  then repeated  at the end for those reading all the way through. It should state exactly what you want subscribers to do, for example "Click here to download the premium theme for free.




6. Is email marketing still effective?

Email marketing is one of the most effective ways for a business to reach its customers directly. Think about it. You don't post something on your site  hoping people will visit it. You don't even post something on a social media page and hope fans  see it. You're sending something straight to each person's inbox, where they'll definitely  see it! Even if they don't open it, they'll still see your subject line and business name every time you send an email, so you're still communicating directly with your audience.



7. However do I grow my email subscribers list? Should i buy an email list or build it myself?

Buying an email list is  waste of time & money. These email accounts are unverified and not interested in your brand. The mailing list is useless if your subscribers do not open your emails. There are different ways to grow your mailing list. 

Give them a free ebook and host it on a landing page where they have to enter the email to download the file and also create a forum page on your website, asks your visitors what questions they might have about your business, and collects email addresses to follow up with them.


8. How do I prevent audience from unsubscribing?


If the  subject line of the email is irrelevant to  customers, they will ignore it multiple times. But, if it keeps repeating, they are intercepted and unsubscribed from your emails. So, send relevant emails for the benefit of the customer. Don't send emails that often only focus  on sales, offers and discounts. 
Submit information about your business and offers so you can connect with customers. You can also update them on recent trends in your industry. The basic role of an email is first and foremost to  connect with customers, get the most out of this tool.

9. What is the difference between a cold email and a spam email?


Cold emails are mostly sales emails that are sent with content align to the needs of the recipient. It is usually personalized and includes a business perspective. However, it is still an unsolicited email. And all unsolicited emails are marked as SPAM. 
Regularly receiving this type of unsolicited email in your users' inboxes, chances are  your emails will soon be diverted to  spam or junk folders. The most important thing to prevent this from happening is to respect your recipients' choice to opt-out of receiving emails from you. You can add the links to easily unsubscribe. You must be familiar with the CAN-SPAM Act and its regulations.

10. Where can I find email template?

Almost all email campaign tools provide you with ready-made templates. Whether you use MailChimp or Pardot, you'll get several email templates ready to use.
 However, if you want to create a template from scratch, you can do so.Most of email campaign tools have option to paste the HTML code of your own design. 


11. What email marketing trend will help marketers succeed in 2022?

Is it a trend to listen to  and get to know your customers? I think people realize how bad it feels for a brand or a company to obsess over themselves without knowing their customers personal needs. People who listen empathetically and then provide value based on what they learn will win.


Final Saying


 You can approach email marketing in different ways. We have compiled a list of most frequently asked questions to help you understand how to get started, what constraints you need to keep in mind, and what future development you will need, we don’t have 100% answers to every situation and there’s always a chance you will have something new and different to deal with as you market your own business.
