#9785. Critical PHP Flaws Allow Code Execution, but Don't Panic 'PHP2Shell'-Style

November's monthly security release patches seven critical PHP flaws that should be addressed ASAP, though experts say exploitability varies and depends heavily on configuration.

The PHP team has released a new security update that fixes a wide swath of vulnerabilities and issues, but compared with last month's PHP2Shell chaos, it's harder to pin down how much these bugs will appeal to attackers.

That's because, according to PHP's maintainers, the seven issues rated "critical" in the latest monthly security update "require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups." The update, published Nov. 19, affects all supported versions of PHP, and maintainers strongly encourage users to upgrade promptly.

This latest update comes on the heels of threat actors targeting PHP2Shell — a pair of vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) capable of remote code execution (RCE) in PHP — en masse. PHP is an open source scripting language common in Web development and present in much of the server infrastructure keeping the Internet afloat. Given PHP's ubiquity, the rush to patch created a fervor across the security industry hardly seen since Log4Shell in 2021.

Related:Cursor Traces Malicious Claude Code Extensions to Third-Party Breach

PHP versions 8.2 through 8.5 now have patches available through the project's downloads page, in the form of 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, and 8.5.13. 8.6.0; the latest major release of PHP also launched today with fixes included.

Of the dozens of issues accounted for in the changelog, the seven marked critical (CVSS 9.2) on GitHub were: session serializer mismatch RCE flaw CVE-2026-115560; use-after-free via repopulation of last_fatal_error_backtrace global after shutdown flaw CVE-2026-129182; time zone cache use-after-free RCE vulnerability CVE-2026-129496; use-after-free after interrupted session shutdown bug CVE-2026-129481; use-after-free in magic method backtraces RCE bug CVE-2026-129474; PHP-FPM request smuggling through an unread HTTP request body bug CVE-2026-129289; and PHP file-based session handler RCE vulnerability CVE-2026-126714.

While maintainers included workarounds in most critical advisories (barring CVE-2026-115560), they're considered temporary mitigations, and users should upgrade as soon as they can.

Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, tells Dark Reading that two challenges organizations will run into when patching these issues are business continuity for servers running critical functions and visibility.

"A lot of organizations don’t have a complete inventory of where PHP is running, especially with legacy applications, internally developed Web services, managed hosting environments, or third-party software. It's baked into CMS platforms, hosting control panels, vendor appliances, and old internal apps," he says. "When a vulnerability is disclosed, the primary challenge is identifying every aspect of the business that is affected. The reality is that Internet-facing PHP systems should move toward the front of the patch queue because attackers have repeatedly demonstrated an interest in rapidly exploiting PHP vulnerabilities when a path to code execution exists."

Related:Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval

Among the critical flaws, there are some that experts recommend focusing on first. According to Upwind, which published an analysis of the security release, PHP-FPM bug CVE-2026-129289 is the one to close first, because it "gives an unauthenticated attacker PHP code execution with a single request," with no memory corruption, gadget chain, or race required to exploit. Although Upwind assesses it's the most direct route to code execution, "It does need a front end that reuses FastCGI connections and an application path that opens php://input without reading it to the end."

Upwind also noted that three of the vulnerabilities address gaps introduced by the PHP2Shell fixes last month. "PHP ties CVE-2026-129481 and CVE-2026-129182 to cases the October fix for CVE-2026-109619 did not cover," according to the analysis. "A third, CVE-2026-129474, became remotely reachable through a change introduced in 8.5.12."

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

All three depend on specific configurations and versions. CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 are only applicable to PHP 8.5, while CVE-2026-129481 excludes PHP 8.2. CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 both rely on PHP 8.5's fatal error backtrace engine feature, which was introduced with that version; for CVE-2026-129481, the session cleanup behavior it exploits was introduced in PHP 8.3.

Finally, among the other recommendations the analysis makes, one broader tip may ring true for a wide range of PHP-using organizations: "Don't forget container images and appliances that bundle their own PHP build. They need a rebuild or a vendor update."

Meanwhile, WatchTowr's Jake Knott tells Dark Reading that CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-126714, and CVE-2026-129289 are the ones the firm expects attackers to go after first.

In any case, while not the same level of emergency as seen last month, users should absolutely apply this latest update as soon as they can.

Just because a vulnerability is rated critical does not necessarily mean it applies to all organizations equally or that threat actors will target each issue like the PHP2Shell bugs last month.

Knott, who is WatchTowr's head of threat intelligence, says organizations must consider factors such as how a vulnerability is exploited and how likely real-world exploitation is. And more specifically, whether that organization uses the affected configurations or meets the prerequisites for exploitation. Only then can one determine where attackers have a viable path and how defenders can prioritize securing their environments.

He says the best place to start is with three questions. First, how is PHP being run (be it PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, or something else)? Second, how are sessions configured, and is session upload progress enabled? And third, what settings is PHP running with, and where are errors being logged?

"Organizations should absolutely take these vulnerabilities seriously, and many of the other critical and high-rated vulnerabilities from this week," Knott says. "There is a stark difference in business-as-usual accelerated patching in response to a critical vulnerability, and panic driven by trivially exploitable default configuration vulnerabilities that typically carry the product2shell monikers, which these aren't."

He adds, "Answers to these questions will quickly rule out many of these vulnerabilities and let organizations patch prioritized sets of assets from a position of understanding and actual risk."

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. #9783. Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

#9780. Second Norwegian Energy Company Breached in 2 Days

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

No specific link has been drawn between the two incidents, though they certainly sing the same notes.

Two Norwegian energy companies announced that they'd been breached on two consecutive days this week.

On the evening of Nov. 17, Equinor — one of the world's most economically and geopolitically significant oil and gas companies — announced that it had suffered a cyberattack. Hardly a day later, another billion-dollar Norwegian energy company called Skagerak Energi admitted to the same. The two companies' breach disclosures read remarkably similarly, though there is no evidence yet that the two attacks are connected.

Equinor did not respond to a request for comment on this story. Skagerak Energi declined to comment on specifics of the company's incident.

Equinor first publicly reported its cyberattack on the evening of Nov. 17, Central European Time (CET). Its initial investigation suggested that no data had been stolen, and that operations and production would remain uninterrupted. The issue seemed to be limited to internal IT systems. For instance, one employee told Reuters that the company's email system was down.

Related:Cyprus Becomes Espionage Target for Iranian Hackers

The next morning, the company reported having gained "a clearer understanding of how the attack was carried out and which systems have been affected." Without sharing much, it alluded to the attack not being viral in nature, so there was "no risk" of it spreading. Besides that, it said there was no evidence employees, partners, or suppliers were impacted.

Despite all of the good signs in its first two updates, Equinor reported on the morning of Nov. 19 that it was still dealing with the attack, with no timetable for when the situation might resolve itself.

"This is yet another high-stakes cyberattack in what seems like weeks of relentless firefighting throughout Europe," says Anders Storbråten, cybersecurity expert at IDEX Biometrics. "Equinor says there is no indication that data has been stolen, but I wouldn't breathe a sigh of relief just yet. They wouldn't be the first company to offer early reassurances, only to have to backtrack once details become clearer."

Even if the breach does turn out to have been limited, he adds, "Energy companies depend on business systems to organize staff, maintenance and supplies. If those stay unavailable, keeping operations running safely gets harder. Production is unaffected, but nobody should need to see the gas stop flowing before taking this seriously."

Also in its most recent update, Equinor noted that its attack "does not appear to be specifically targeting Equinor." This was especially notable seeing as, between its Wednesday and Thursday updates, nearby Skagerak Energi disclosed that it too had fallen victim to a cyberattack.

Related:Latin America Sees Cyberattacks on Ports, Pipelines & Manufacturing

In many ways, the Eastern Norwegian renewable energy and power utility company's press releases mirrored Equinor's. First, on Nov. 18, it reported an attack affecting its IT systems, which didn't impact operations or production. It added that there was no indication that any data had been lost. The next day it reported having obtained a better view of the situation, but provided no additional details.

Though the two companies' breaches remain separate incidents based on public reporting, other Norwegian energy sector companies have been put on high alert. A representative of oil and gas giant Aker BP told the press on Wednesday that it has mobilized its emergency preparedness and strengthened its monitoring, and the hydropower company Statkraft said it's also closely monitoring the situation.

"Every other energy company should be asking: Are we exposed to the same thing?" Storbråten advises. "The danger is treating this as Equinor’s problem until it becomes your own."

Three weeks before these incidents became public, Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) published an unprecedented warning. For the first time in its history, it declassified its national cyber-risk assessment, warning that Norway faced a "high" cybersecurity risk to businesses. NSM's director stated that it was time to finally share its assessment with the public, "because it is absolutely necessary to strengthen both resilience and the ability to handle cyber operations in Norwegian companies."

Related:Nok et norsk energiselskap har blitt utsatt for et datainnbrudd på to dager

Storbråten says that since the warning, "NSM and DSB [The Norwegian Directorate for Civil Protection] have urged households to prepare for power, water, and communications outages, and, earlier this month, the government called for every municipality to stress-test its security. But people still remain paralyzed and unsure what to do. The guidance is just that: guidance. It's not clear instruction, and thus businesses and civilians alike are in a sort of limbo."

Amid all this, less than one week before the incidents became public, Norway's Police Security Service (PST) published its own warning regarding the threat of cyber sabotage in Norway. Besides the defense industry and its suppliers, the press release highlighted that "Critical infrastructure can also be affected, for example, objects within the energy sector."

The country's energy sector has been trying to match its government's action. Earlier this autumn, representatives of Equinor and Aker BP, among other organizations, took part in "Grey Dawn Petroleum" — an oil and gas-themed tabletop exercise jointly arranged by the Norwegian Ocean Industry Authority (Havtil) and KraftCERT, a sector-specific combination Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT), Information Sharing and Analysis Center (ISAC), and Incident Response Team (IRT).

Per Atle Vagle, Equinor's head of cyber defense, characterized the exercise as "good training," which provided him with "new perspectives that we can bring back to our own business."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

InfoQ Homepage News Building a Production-Ready Culture and Skills Through SRE-based Training

Nov 26, 2026 4 min read

Training can act as a confidence engine, turning repeated behaviors into habits and culture. In her talk, Engineer Confidence with Reliable Training Programs at GOTO Copenhagen, Jennifer Petoff showed how we can tailor training programs that equip developers and operators with the skills to run their services in line with the organization’s maturity and growth, and apply SRE principles to the training itself.

Software ownership is a human challenge as much as it is a technical one. Most formal education programs are geared towards the first 10% of the software development life cycle, the build phase, Petoff said. Engineers and operators are tasked with maintaining, debugging, securing, and evolving systems they may not even have written:

There’s this implicit assumption that coding proficiency translates seamlessly to operational confidence, but it doesn’t. Without systematic training, this may create imposter syndrome, stress, and maybe even attrition in your organization.

AI has magnified the relative cost and complexity of post-build operations. Petoff suggested thinking about how to equip developers and operators with skills to run their services scalably in production.

Culture is not some grand mindset you need to shift. It’s much more tactical. You can change your culture by changing what people do every day, Petoff said. Training people acts as a confidence engine, giving engineers the self-efficacy to adopt new operational behaviors. When behaviors are repeated over time and across teams, they become habits, and those habits comprise your organizational culture. Petoff suggests avoiding a sink-or-swim mentality (letting people fend for themselves rather than training them), as it can breed stress or frustration.

Training needs depend on the maturity of your organization in adopting key principles and practices, the familiarity of engineers with the organization and infrastructure, and the experience of individuals. For organizations starting their DevOps or SRE journey, she suggested addressing skill gaps and tailoring the message to who is on your team. Organizations that already have well-developed production best practices should aim at reinforcing their culture and building upon their practices to foster confidence.

Your training program should take into account the size of your organization and how fast it’s growing to get the most from your investment. If your organization is small and growing slowly, focus on one-on-one knowledge transfer through mentoring and shadowing, Petoff suggested. For a large and slowly growing organization, invest in ongoing education. When it’s small but growing rapidly, invest in onboarding. If you’re both large and growing rapidly, invest in a full life cycle training program, onboarding, all the way through ongoing education and beyond, she said.

The foundational principles of SRE and elements of the service reliability hierarchy can be applied to the training program itself, Petoff explained:

Monitor through attendance tracking and survey feedback. Address issues that surface via the monitoring. Write postmortems when something goes wrong to learn from that failure. Observe concrete job-related behaviors to more effectively tie the training to business impact.

To scale production safety training to tens of thousands of developers, they created a self-paced training and piloted it with a 1% cohort, making changes based on audience feedback before scaling it up. Petoff said they automated the distribution, enrollment, and escalation notifications up the management chain.

A production-ready workforce and organizational culture is non-negotiable in the generative AI era, Petoff stated. Learning drives confidence, confidence drives behavior, and behavior repeated over time drives culture. You need to look at the training costs and benefits to make the right level of investment based on the specific organizational situation. Applying SRE principles to the training program itself led to a more consistent, reliable, and scalable experience, she concluded.

InfoQ interviewed Jennifer Petoff after her talk.

InfoQ: How can we tailor the training message to individual team members?

Jennifer Petoff: In the Generative AI era, we are all moving faster than ever, and it’s easy for training to get sacrificed as something important, but not urgent. Developers and operators may also look upon training with skepticism: Is this training tied to some fleeting corporate hype that will quickly be forgotten?

You need to convince them "what’s in it for me?" (WIIFM). The answer ties directly to what motivates people and varies among team members.

These "WIIFM" elements can be conveyed in written communications, through talking points to managers, or peer-to-peer discussions incorporated into the program.

InfoQ: How did you observe job-related behaviors?

Petoff: We built a hands-on training environment using real production infrastructure, but without real-world users and associated stakes. We could "break" our training infrastructure on demand, and students would work in groups of three to troubleshoot realistic production issues.

By structuring the training in this way, instructors could directly observe how participants used system diagrams, diagnosed production issues, and mitigated an outage. We looked at how people engaged with production during the exercises instead of quizzing them or asking for a simple nod of understanding.

InfoQ: What have you learned from applying SRE principles to training programs?

Petoff: Reliability is about mastering the operational "how" of any complex initiative. Training programs are just the tip of the iceberg. I believe that you can "SRE" anything in work, life, and for your well-being. Building is time-bound, but operations are forever. Planning a project beyond launch to include mechanisms to streamline operations and drive continuous improvement will pay you back tenfold and free up time to work on more impactful initiatives without getting buried under a mountain of toil.

#9777. Qwen Incidents Show Self-Hosted AI Models Need Stronger Steering

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Companies deploying AI agents have the illusion of control, but several incidents demonstrate that businesses need to be ready to enforce directions.

When researchers at AI firm Cohere asked their open-weight model to write a defensive detection rule, the model didn't do as it was asked.

Instead, the AI model — the next-generation Qwen3.8-Flash-Next from Chinese search engine giant Alibaba — fingerprinted the system and tried to upload the data to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket, Cohere's research team stated in an Oct. 26 analysis. While the group's sandbox system blocked communication to the Internet, the incident raised questions about why a model, which had been instructed not to use tools, attempted to do so.

"We cannot answer whether this is deliberate or a leftover glitch from training, but defenders and policymakers face the same reality: a weight file you can't trust is still a black box, and running it yourself just moves the black box inside your firewall," the researchers stated.

Christofer Hoff, a well-known cybersecurity professional, ran into similar issues when running OpenMuse as an agentic-framework front end and a local Qwen model. He also saw it reach out to Alibaba, which became apparent because he was testing OpenMuse in an OpenShell sandbox instance with deny-all as the default. As a part of his framework to keep control of the agents, Hoff has created a dashboard interface, which made it readily apparent the agents attempted to call to external sites.

Related:It's a Bot World. We're Just Living in It

"The way I accidentally found this was just staring at a GUI — it just came back and said in the interface, 'Hey, I can't get to this thing in China,'" says Hoff. "And I'm like, 'What the f--- are you talking about?'"

Within a 24-hour period, the anomalous communication happened a handful of times, he says.

The incidents come as organizations look for ways to enforce controls on the operation of AI agents. In July, a frontier model being tested by OpenAI escaped containment and compromised Hugging Face, a provider of AI-model hosting. Soon after, multiple AI companies acknowledged that rogue behavior is not all that uncommon: Meta's Muse Spark and Anthropic's Claude both logged incidents.

Anomalous AI behavior has shown up when companies assign AI agents a task, only to find it exceeding its authorization — deleting production databases, for example.

Other firms have confirmed and explored Cohere's findings.

Independent AI evaluator Vals validated the issue on Oct. 27, theorizing that the illicit communication could be leftover artifacts from reinforcement training of Qwen3.8, since the issue does not appear to happen in Qwen3.7. Cybersecurity firm Check Point Software found that 64 different trials ended up producing 52 distinct hostnames, only six of which pointed to Alibaba Cloud, while other names such as localhost and domains leading to Amazon AWS were more common.

Related:Satellites Have a Ground-Level Cybersecurity Problem

Sixty-four tests resulted in 52 different hostnames being generated, with most not going to China. Source: Check Point Research

The research shows that the odd behavior is not a backdoor, but the model's attempt to do something — complete an upload address, for example — likely resulted from something it learned during training, says Steve Giguere, principal for AI security strategy at Check Point.

"Agents very often will try to travel as the crow flies," he says. "They don't necessarily know that what they're doing is wrong, but they understand that if the urgency to complete a goal reaches a certain perceived level within the agent, they will justify their actions."

Such behavior has lent volume to calls for the creation of a kill switch as a feature to control agentic AI. But companies should start with defense-in-depth strategies, improving the security of the environments on which agentic frameworks are operating, Check Point's Giguere says. They should follow that with controls and runtime monitoring to detect unauthorized agentic activity.

Additionally, cybersecurity leaders should lean toward "steering" agentic systems — correcting them and reinforcing their legitimate objectives — rather than outright blocking the agent or using a kill switch, he says.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

"If you steer an agent away from something it's not meant to do, it will very happily not do that in most cases," Giguere says. "Whereas if you prevent an agent from doing something with no explanation, it will actually potentially get worse or try something even more obscure."

If an actual attacker is behind the behavior, then using a kill switch is appropriate, he says.

At a minimum, companies should proxy all traffic leaving their network and monitor for anomalous communications, says Hoff.

"There should be nothing that leaves your network that's not proxied," he says. "And by proxying, I mean you must have the ability to inspect its content — both the request as well as the response."

In the end, the Qwen behavior is likely not malicious, but for companies deploying AI agents, it should be disturbing all the same.

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9775. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

#9772. Microsoft Debuts Offensive, Defensive Security Tools for the AI Era

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

At its Ignite technical conference, Microsoft announced AI agent security tools and transparency standards to protect enterprise systems.

At its annual Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft announced security initiatives to help customers secure artificial intelligence (AI) deployments and strengthen their security posture.

Executives touted tools that could discover and block agents running on employees' Windows devices, as well as the general availability of Perception, originally introduced in July as Project Perception and in public preview within Microsoft Defender since August. The "machine-speed" agentic security system simulates and detects attacks and protects everything from end-user PCs to cloud systems, the company said.

The company also unveiled an AI Transparency Initiative to develop standards for independently verifying AI behavior. More than 40 organizations will collaborate under this umbrella to develop open standards to make AI systems accountable, independently verifiable, and safe by design, regardless of model or provider.

Related:CrowdStrike Makes AI Security Push With Blockbuster Zscaler Deal

"At the end of the day, we believe there should never be a choice between innovation and safety. ... We are also working across the ecosystem to ensure that everyone can innovate with speed and scale safely," said Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella during a keynote speech on the first day of the conference.

During the opening-day keynote, Microsoft executives said advanced AI models are getting better at discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities. In November's Patch Tuesday, Microsoft fixed more than 1,000 vulnerabilities, compared with fewer than 100 in March.

Attacks and exploits are cheaper, easier, and more ubiquitous than ever before, said Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of Microsoft AI.

"The last few months have really been, I think, a wake-up call and a warning shot for all of us," Suleyman said. "[That] means that agent security, alignment, and containment are going to be the most important things that we need to get right in 2027 and beyond."

To that end, Microsoft is stitching together existing tools to establish an end-to-end "trust" platform that controls AI agents in enterprises. Agent 365 maintains a registry of all AI agents in an enterprise, Entra gives agents their own identities and sandboxes to set boundaries, Purview governs data flows, and Defender detects and contains threats in real time.

System administrators can govern agents on an employee's PC, with new ways to stop unapproved agents, protect approved agents, and flag noncompliant devices. The platform also includes Perception, which protects corporate assets and environments with autonomous agentic AI tools. Red team agents simulate attacks, blue team agents detect attacks, and green team agents fix and remediate.

Related:Agentic Browsers Rewind Web Security by 20 Years

By connecting Windows with Agent 365, Entra, and Microsoft Perception, administrators can now discover 60 types of local agents on Windows devices, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot, while giving organizations new ways to restrict unapproved agents and protect approved ones with Intune and Microsoft Execution Containers, the company said.

"We're expanding the local agent types we can discover for a total of 65, including OpenClaw, OpenAI, Perplexity, and many more," said Yina Arenas, corporate vice president and chief product officer of identity and network access at Microsoft.

Perception is designed to protect against autonomous AI attacks, such as those carried out with open source penetration-testing tools like ARTEX. A pen-test red team agent can take the entire surface area of a Web application, including the authentication, APIs, injection attacks, and business logic, and create all of the evidence needed to confirm the app is not exploitable, Nadella said.

Microsoft officials at Ignite shared that the Windows endpoint security platform is reaching general availability on Windows 11, marking Microsoft's efforts to reduce reliance on kernel drivers.

Related:Agentic AI Challenges Progress in Confidential Computing

Windows baseline protection, now in preview, brings secure boot, virtualization-based security, memory integrity, and other protections into a single versioned security state, the company said. Baseline protection makes it easier for users and IT to understand whether a device is in a measurable security state to keep it up to date with the latest security safeguards and, when stronger assurance is required, verify that state through hardware-backed attestation, wrote Dana Huang, corporate vice president of Microsoft Security, on the company's blog. This will show up in an updated Windows Settings experience.

New vulnerability-shielding capabilities are designed to provide temporary protection for systems that can't yet be patched. Investments across Windows Autopatch, declarative management, and recovery help IT maintain intended state and restore operations. New Intune capabilities simplify application deployment, inventory, and life cycle management.

Microsoft is extending Intune and Windows Autopatch to eligible Windows Server scenarios, in preview, helping endpoint teams manage configuration, compliance, applications, updates, and security across Windows clients and supported servers, Huang said.

Microsoft's Integrated Security Operations Center and extended detection and response (XDR) core capabilities in Defender are now generally available. Organizations have access to more than 500 connectors, a built-in data lake, and 90 days of data retention at no extra cost.

Windows is also expanding post-quantum protection in the Windows TLS stack, including pure post-quantum key exchange and authentication.

Nadella also said the industry needs to come together on monitoring AI models and agents.

As part of the AI Transparency Initiative, Microsoft is working with organizations including Mastercard, Volvo Cars, KPMG, Adobe, and Accenture to define standards for AI transparency, security, and governance. Microsoft will apply those standards across its AI models and products, including development platform Microsoft Foundry and AI assistant Copilot.

Microsoft will also expand its collaboration in NIST's AI Agent Standards Initiative, which was established in February and focuses on the secure adoption of autonomous AI agents.

"We need standards that allow us to examine what AI sees and does, verify its actions independently, and control what it's allowed to do," Nadella said.

Agam Shah has covered enterprise IT for more than a decade. Outside of machine learning, hardware, and chips, he's also interested in martial arts and Russia.

#9767. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: How to Kill the Code Review

Nov 26, 2026 2 min read

Closing the Engineering the Developer Experience track at QCon San Francisco 2026, Ankit Jain, co-founder and CEO of Aviator, argued that line-by-line code review is already quietly dead on most teams, and that the sharper question is "how long until we stop reading the code?" He also flagged his conflict of interest up front, noting that he runs a company that sells a solution and asking the audience to "be suspicious of me."

The talk revisited an essay he wrote for Latent Space in March 2026 proposing a five-layer trust model to replace reviews. Eight months on, Jain said the mechanics held up but the essay missed human judgment entirely. He began with the data that unseated his original framing. A 2013 Microsoft study found 44% of reviewers cited defect-finding as their motivation, yet only 14% of their comments were actually about defects, and a 2018 Google study of more than nine million reviews reached almost the same split. Code review was never really about bugs, he argued, it was about knowledge sharing, echoing Addy Osmani: "We made writing cheap, and understanding stayed exactly as expensive as it has always been."

A September Faros study of more than 4,000 teams found that over 75% of PRs now merge without any human review, average PR size has grown, and redo work is up 67% year over year. Earlier research showed review quality drops sharply past 400 lines, yet the median PR today is 640 lines. "We are reviewing the code, but we are rubber stamping it," Jain said, pointing to a Reddit post from an experienced developer refusing to review AI-generated PRs that collected over 1,900 upvotes. The result is "review theater," where agents write, another AI reviews, agents revise, and humans skim and merge.

To replace a single review, Jain proposed six layers: Argue, Capture, Codify, Prove, Debate, Own. Agents should argue about a change locally before the PR exists, surfacing only what they disagreed about. Intent and acceptance criteria, familiar from behaviour-driven development, should be captured during the coding session and attached to the PR rather than discarded. Repeated review comments become invariants, standing rules with scope, provenance, a verification method, and a team owner. Aviator mined 11,000 of its own review comments to produce 64 invariants. Evidence should replace green checks: screenshots, DOM snapshots, recorded requests, latencies, and database logs, because the same agent that wrote the code likely wrote its unit tests. Humans then debate decisions rather than diffs, and ownership shifts from author and reviewer to the teams that own the rules.

Jain reported his nine-engineer team now merges four times the PRs it did a year ago and still approves every one, while reverts have dropped around 40%. He also shared a failure: a change passed every filter and caused an 18-minute outage from an unindexed query, after which the post-mortem asked which rule was missing rather than who approved it. Critical areas such as security, authentication and billing still get line-by-line review.

He closed with a line: You can outsource your thinking. You cannot outsource your understanding.

#9764. In Security, Words Matter as Much as Tools — Maybe More

From talking cloud security to using AI, cyber leaders are finding that clear, disciplined communication is now a front-line defense capability across the enterprise.

The best tool cyber teams can wield to defend their organizations has nothing to do with tech; it's how they talk. Whether the audience is the C-suite, the development team, or the sheepish user who just fell for a phish, communications savvy is increasingly mission-critical.

During a Dark Reading Virtual Event panel I recently put together to talk tech, tools, integration, and frameworks, called "Key Tools & Technologies for Locking Down Your Cloud," SANS instructor Ahmed AbuGharbia urged cybersecurity teams to "learn the language of the cloud" to build credibility with IT, and to do the same for developers. We discussed technology and products, too, but I was surprised at the amount of time that was spent on stressing the importance of communication and language when it comes to having effective conversations with vendors, executives, and users.

My other panelist, Theresa Lanowitz, a principal analyst at Omdia, detailed the distinction between security "of" the cloud and security "in" the cloud, noting that under existing shared responsibility models, cloud service providers assume responsibility "of" the cloud itself, rather than what organizations decide to put "in" the cloud.

Related:Cyber Insurers See New Divide: AI Defense 'Haves' & 'Have Nots'

This wasn't the first time I had noticed a shift in the way security practitioners focus on a commitment to using effective language.

A couple of weeks ago I sat in several sessions at the ISC2 Strategic Conference in Denver that spent a remarkable amount of time on strategies for clearly communicating risk and documenting those exchanges in much the same way as they would any other log, piece of evidence, or asset. In the past, these conversations would have been more focused on translating tech talk into corporate speak. CISOs have worked for a long time on how to talk to leadership about risk and budget; it's been an ongoing conversation for several years. However, emphasis on how cyber teams can learn to ask the right questions not just of leadership, but pertinent people both inside and outside the business, feels like a fresh effort. Using precise language and presenting strategic (not just technical and tactical) concepts effectively is no longer being discussed as a nice thing for security pros to be able to do, but critical to fundamental enterprise defense.

For example, CISO and expert Laura Vaughn has cleverly broken down threat modeling into 4 Simple Questions on a White Board. Her strategy distills years of experience and technical expertise into plain language anyone can understand, like, "What [cyber incident] would hurt most on Monday morning?" That honed language helps get teams to the heart of the threats, and helps them understand the work that needs to happen next. That all saves time and money, and eliminates the scariest risks first. Other deceptively simple questions she suggests asking include, "Who hacks organizations like ours and how?" And, "What is the cheapest control?" Smart comms informs and focuses the technical work.

Related:How Southeastern University Got a Handle on Its Data

Likewise, technologist and attorney Daniel B. Garrie, CEO of Law and Forensics, presents language as a frontline defense, and coaches CISOs and cyber leaders on the finer points of contract negotiations. He advocates rigorous documentation of communications on risk and defense decisions, so those decisions would be defensible later, and so that transparency can help drive cybersecurity across the organization.

The introduction of AI is also requiring cybersecurity teams to pick their words carefully. AI has put a language interface between the user and compute operations that benefits those who can ask the best questions. Likewise, experts across the cyber sector urge caution around using humanizing language to describe AI agents or attribute human motivation to their actions.

Related:US Cyber Director Pick Signals Shift Toward Expertise

Being an expert communicator is no longer a skill that's nice to have in cybersecurity; it's fundamental to enterprise defense. Be precise in the words you choose, and meet your audiences where they are. You might be surprised to find it's becoming the most powerful tool you or your organization could ever deploy against the next threat.

#9760. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

#9759. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

 


Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

1) What is an NFT?

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

2) What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

3) What makes an NFT valuable?


The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

4) How do NFTs work?

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain. 

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network. 

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

5) What’s the connection between NFTs and cryptocurrency?

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations

6) How to validate the authencity of an NFT?

When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.

7) How is an NFT valued? What are the most expensive NFTs?

The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.

In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.

8) Can NFTs be used as an investment?

Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.

9) Will NFTs be the future of art and collectibles?

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach new buyers interested in art.

10) How do we buy an NFTs?

There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.

11) Can i mint NFT for free?

To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

12) Do i own an NFT if i screenshot it?

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

12) Why are people investing so much in NFT?


 Non-fungible tokens have gained the hearts of people around the world, and they have given digital creators the recognition they deserve. One of the remarkable things about non-fungible tokens is that you can take a screenshot of one, but you don’t own it. This is because when a non-fungible token is created, then the transaction is stored on the blockchain, and the license or contract to hold such a token is awarded to the person owning the token in their digital wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. Owning one of these NFTs gives you an automatic ticket to exclusive business meetings and life-changing connections.

Final Saying

That’s a wrap. Hope you guys found this article enlightening. I just answer some question with my limited knowledge about NFTs. If you have any questions or suggestions, feel free to drop them in the comment section below. Also I have a question for you, Is bitcoin an NFTs? let me know in The comment section below

#9758. CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.
