#9757. The 20 Best Local LLMs of 2026: A Complete Guide for Enterprises and Power Users

The | Gen AI | AI Agents | AI Tools | SLMs | LLMs | Engineer | Quantum | Research | Developer | Python | Go | Rust | Mastery Playbook.

The | Gen AI | AI Agents | AI Tools | SLMs | LLMs | Engineer | Quantum | Research | Developer | Python | Go | Rust | Mastery Playbook.

The | Gen AI | AI Agents | AI Tools | SLMs | LLMs | Engineer | Quantum | Research | Developer | Python | Go | Rust | Mastery Playbook.

Your provider changed its usage caps again.

Your legal team will not let customer data touch a third-party API.

Your best engineer hit a rate limit in the middle of a production incident.

Most CTOs, founders and serious AI users have lived at least one of these lines this year.

That is why it’s high time every enterprise worldwide tool Local AI seriously.

Open-weight models crossed a threshold in 2026.

Kimi K3.1 Pro, GLM-5.3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Muse Spark Open and Mistral Large 4 now trade blows with the closed frontier, and every one of them can be downloaded today.

Put the right model on the right hardware, and the token meter simply stops running.

This guide ranks 20 open-weight models in two Top Ten lists.

The first list is for enterprises running four 512 GB Mac Studios joined over Thunderbolt 5 into a 2,048 GB pool of unified memory.

The second is for power users with a single machine and at least 64 GB of VRAM or unified memory.

You will get parameter counts, architectures, published benchmarks, quantized and uncensored Hugging Face releases, a full quantization primer, two detailed budgets, and the security case for running all of this yourself.

If you are interested in Local LLMs, and saving your API bills (or eliminating them entirely) you need to read this!

Cloud AI is priced like electricity from a landlord.

You pay per token, you accept the landlord's rules, and the landlord can change the price whenever it likes.

Local AI turns that per-token bill into a capacity bill you own.

You pay once for hardware, then a modest amount for power, and the marginal cost of the next million tokens is close to zero.

Here is what changes the day your model runs on your own silicon:

Within the throughput of your hardware, yes - and that distinction matters, which is why this guide spends so much time on memory, bandwidth and money.

The core rule of local inference is simple.

Capacity decides which models fit, and bandwidth decides how fast they run.

You cannot talk about local AI without talking about quantization.

It is the single technique that turns a 1.6 terabyte download into something that fits on a desk.

But first - what the heck is quantization anyway?

Every model is a giant collection of numbers called weights. At training time each weight is usually stored in 16-bit or 32-bit floating point.

Quantization stores those same weights with fewer bits. Fewer bits per weight means less memory, less data to move per token, and therefore faster generation on bandwidth-bound hardware like Apple Silicon.

Push the bit count too low and the model starts to forget facts, lose track of long instructions, and make sloppy tool calls.

Add roughly 10 to 30 percent on top for the KV cache, runtime buffers and the operating system.

A 70-billion-parameter model at 4.5 bits per weight needs about 39 GB for weights alone.

The key difference from older 4-bit schemes is quantization-aware training.

When a lab trains the model to live in 4 bits from the start, the quality loss largely disappears.

GGUF is the file format of llama.cpp, and by extension Ollama, LM Studio and Jan. Its quant names look cryptic, but they follow a pattern.

The "K" means super-blocks with nested scales, and the S, M and L suffixes mean small, medium and large. The M and L variants keep sensitive tensors such as attention and output layers at higher precision.

When you see "i1-GGUF" in a repository name, such as the mradermacher releases, that means imatrix-calibrated files.

Unsloth's Dynamic 2.0 quants (names like UD-Q4_K_XL or UD-IQ1_S) do not give every layer the same precision.

They keep critical layers at higher bit widths and crush the bulk of the MoE experts harder.

That is how Unsloth lists a 1-bit Mistral Large 4 at about 233 GB and a 1-bit Kimi K3 at about 594 GB, as reported in an M5 Ultra hosting guide.

Unsloth itself claims around 91 percent top-1 agreement for its smallest Mistral Large 4 quant, which is a vendor claim, so test it on your own prompts.

Apple's MLX framework has its own group-wise quantization at 3, 4, 6 and 8 bits, published under the mlx-community organisation on Hugging Face.

On Apple Silicon, MLX is often noticeably faster than llama.cpp for the same model.

One measured comparison on an M5 Ultra found DeepSeek V4 Flash at about 40 tokens per second under llama.cpp and about 53 tokens per second under MLX, according to an M5 Ultra benchmark.

That is roughly a third more speed from a software switch.

The KV cache stores the attention keys and values for every token in your context.

At a million tokens of context it can rival the weights in size.

Both llama.cpp and MLX can store the KV cache in 8-bit or 4-bit.

An 8-bit KV cache is nearly free in quality and halves context memory, while 4-bit is more aggressive and worth testing on long-document tasks first.

DeepSeek says V4.1 Flash cuts its KV cache to about a quarter of V4 Flash's, and hybrid linear-attention designs like Qwen's Gated DeltaNet and Kimi's Delta Attention shrink it further.

Dense models below 40B: stay at Q5_K_M or higher.

Mid-size MoE models: Q4_K_M or MLX 4-bit.

Trillion-parameter MoE models: whatever fits, because a 2-bit giant often beats an 8-bit dwarf.

They come straight out of the file sizes of the models that matter in late 2026.

Kimi K3.1 Pro is a 2.8-trillion-parameter model that downloads at about 1.56 TB in its native MXFP4 format, as confirmed in a Kimi K3.1 Pro weights report.

Mistral Large 4 is about 1,060 GB in official FP8, and Muse Spark Open needs about 1.63 TB in full BF16.

A single 512 GB Mac Studio cannot hold any of these at high precision.

Two machines (1,024 GB) hold some of them at 4-bit.

Four machines (2,048 GB) hold every one of them at its native or near-native precision, with room left over.

That headroom is not waste. It goes to three jobs:

Four is also the natural size for a Thunderbolt 5 mesh.

Each Mac Studio can cable directly to the other three, so every node is one hop from every other node, and there is no switch to buy or fail.

Apple added RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 in macOS 26.2, and Jeff Geerling's cluster test showed exo with RDMA speeding up as nodes were added while llama.cpp over TCP slowed down.

On Qwen3 235B, exo went from 19.5 tokens per second on one node to 31.9 on four, according to AppleInsider's write-up.

With the 2026 M5 Ultra, each node brings 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth.

Four of them reach about 4.8 TB/s in aggregate, a figure exo Labs highlights in its four Mac cluster announcement.

Why 512 GB nodes rather than eight 256 GB nodes?

TechRepublic notes that two 256 GB Mac Studios cost about $700 less than one 512 GB machine, so smaller nodes are cheaper per gigabyte.

But eight nodes cannot form a direct mesh, every extra hop adds synchronisation latency, and every extra box adds cables, power bricks and failure points.

The 2026 mid-size models are astonishingly good.

Qwen3.8-27B posts 61.7 on SWE-bench Pro, and its 4-bit build is only about 17 GB, according to a Qwen3.8-27B analysis.

Because the floor is about running the best small models well, not just running them.

One hundred and twenty-eight is the sweet spot.

Hardware: four Mac Studios with M5 Ultra and 512 GB of unified memory each, cabled as a Thunderbolt 5 mesh with RDMA enabled, for 2,048 GB of pooled memory and about 4.8 TB/s of aggregate bandwidth.

Ranking rule: most powerful in real-world usability first. I weigh output quality, agentic and tool-calling reliability, speed on this cluster, licence freedom and context length - not raw benchmark scores alone.

A word on benchmarks: almost every number below is vendor-reported, and labs use different harnesses. Treat cross-lab comparisons as directional, not as gospel.

Moonshot AI's Kimi K3.1 Pro is the most capable open-weight model you can download as of late November 2026.

Why rank 1: nothing else open-weight matches its combination of agentic depth, million-token context and multimodal input. It is the slowest model on this list - and the smartest.

Z.ai's GLM-5.3 is the coding and cybersecurity specialist of the open frontier.

If your enterprise writes software, this is the model your engineers will fight over.

Its successor, GLM-5.4, arrived on 23 November as Z.ai's first Loop Transformer, running 28 layers of the GLM-5 base twice at about 750B parameters.

It is hosted-only for now, Z.ai has published no benchmark scores for it, and weights will follow safety hardening, per The Next Web.

Until they ship, GLM-5.3 is the GLM you can own.

Why rank 2: on coding and terminal work it sits right next to the closed frontier, it runs faster than Kimi because only 40B parameters are active, and its licence is practically unrestricted.

DeepSeek did something unusual in September 2026.

It released a "Flash" model and then retired its own flagship because the Flash model beat it.

Why rank 3: MIT licence, million-token context, vision, and near-frontier agentic scores at a fraction of the active compute. It is the model that serves the most people per watt.

Inkling 2 Small is the newest model on this list, and it replaces Inkling-Small outright. Thinking Machines built it as a base for agents that plan, call tools and check their own results - chat quality came second.

Why rank 4: Apache 2.0 weights, a million-token context, vision and agentic scores just behind DeepSeek V4.1 Flash - all at 17B active. It is the strongest permissively licensed agent model on this list.

Alibaba's Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B is the open-weight release of Qwen3.8-Max, and the first time Qwen has opened a Max-tier model.

Why rank 5: enormous knowledge capacity and strong reasoning, held back from a higher rank only by the text-only open checkpoint and the need to quantize it.

Mistral Large 4, nicknamed "Le Chonk", is Europe's trillion-parameter answer, trained from scratch on Mistral's own European infrastructure.

Why rank 6: a trillion-parameter model with a clean commercial licence for in-house use and the strongest sovereignty story in this list for European buyers.

Meta's Muse Spark Open is the most capable US open-weight model to date, and it was built with the Mac Studio in mind.

Why rank 7: the fastest measured giant on this exact hardware and the best tool-user in the list, held back by its licence and by trailing the top three on hard coding.

Thinking Machines Lab, founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, released Inkling as a broad, balanced base for enterprises to shape themselves.

Why rank 8: Apache 2.0, audio input and a design built for customisation make it the deepest foundation for a proprietary in-house model, though the newer Inkling 2 Small is the better pick if you do not need audio.

MiniMax M3 is the long-context efficiency specialist of the group.

Why rank 9: the most efficient million-token model here, small enough to run on a single node at 4-bit.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is Alibaba's early preview of the Qwen4 architecture, and it is brutally efficient.

Why rank 10: it does not compete with the giants on depth, but it lets one cluster serve hundreds of quick requests while the giants think.

Inkling-Small (276B, 12B active, about 552 GB in BF16), now superseded by Inkling 2 Small but still a light fine-tuning base, per the Inkling-Small model card; GLM-5.4 (about 750B), which is live on Z.ai's Coding Plan but has no open weights yet; GLM-5.3-Flash (320B, 18B active), NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL (120B, 12B active), and Meituan's LongCat-2.5 (1.6T, about 48B active, MIT), whose model card currently documents deployment only on NPUs.

Hardware: one system with at least 64 GB of VRAM or unified memory. Think Ryzen AI Max+ 395 mini PCs, NVIDIA DGX Spark, M5 Max or M5 Ultra Mac Studios, or a workstation with an RTX PRO 6000.

Ranking rule: usability first. For a single machine that means quality per gigabyte, speed, tool-calling reliability, licence freedom, and the availability of good quantized and uncensored builds.

Memory tier notes: each entry lists the smallest tier that runs it comfortably, so you can see at a glance what your own machine can handle.

The best local model you can run on a single consumer machine in late 2026 is a 27-billion-parameter dense model.

Why rank 1: frontier-class agentic scores, Apache 2.0, a tiny memory footprint, and some of the most downloaded abliterated releases on Hugging Face.

DeepSeek V4 Flash has been retired from DeepSeek's API in favour of V4.1 Flash, but its MIT-licensed weights remain one of the best things a single large-memory machine can run.

Local performance: about 53 tokens per second under MLX and 40 under llama.cpp on an M5 Ultra.

Why rank 2: the strongest MIT-licensed model a single machine can hold at 4-bit. It only drops below Qwen3.8-27B because it needs four to eight times the memory.

Inkling 2 Mini is the smallest model in Thinking Machines' second generation, and it brings a new idea to the desktop: a looped transformer.

Why rank 3: the most agentic capability per gigabyte on this list, with Apache 2.0 weights and a million-token context. It sits behind Qwen3.8-27B, which matches it on the Intelligence Index with a more mature uncensored ecosystem, and behind DeepSeek V4 Flash on raw depth.

Google DeepMind's Gemma 4 31B is the strongest Western dense model you can run on a laptop-class machine.

Why rank 4: outstanding reasoning per gigabyte and a mature uncensored ecosystem, but weaker than Qwen on agentic software engineering, scoring 52.0 on SWE-bench Verified in Qwen's comparison table.

OpenAI's gpt-oss-120b is more than a year old, and it is still on this list. That tells you how well it was built.

Why rank 5: rock-solid tool calling and the most battle-tested uncensored variants in the list, held back by a shorter context window and its age.

Mistral Small 4 is three models in one: Magistral reasoning, Pixtral vision and Devstral coding, merged into a single MoE.

Why rank 6: the most versatile single model at this size, with a configurable reasoning effort that keeps answers short when you want speed.

Three billion active parameters should not be able to do this.

Why rank 7: the best speed-to-intelligence ratio in the power-user list.

The largest Apache-licensed Qwen MoE that fits comfortably in 128 GB.

Why rank 8: best-in-class tool use for its size, though the newer Qwen3.8-27B now beats it on coding.

Meta's return to open weights started small, and small turned out to be very good.

Why rank 9: a strong American Apache-licensed option that beats Gemma 4 31B on software engineering, though Qwen still leads on terminal and computer-use work.

NVIDIA squeezed a 74-billion-parameter agent model into 24 GB. On a 64 GB machine that leaves an enormous budget for context.

Why rank 10: the fastest agent in the list on NVIDIA hardware, but its intelligence index trails the Qwen and Gemma models above it.

Gemma 4 26B A4B (25.2B, 3.8B active, Apache 2.0), still brilliant at reasoning per watt but weak at agentic coding, with imatrix GGUFs from mradermacher of its abliterated build; Devstral Small 2 (24B, Apache 2.0, a focused local coding agent), Olmo 3.1 32B (fully open training data), and Inkling 2 Small for anyone with a 512 GB machine, where bartowski's Q4_K_M build (about 369 GB) fits with room for context.

Memory figures marked with a tilde are approximate weight sizes from model cards, quant repositories and the guides cited above, before KV cache. "n/a" means no published figure I could verify.

Prices below are US list prices as of November 2026; items marked "estimate" are my planning figures, not quotes, so get real quotes before you buy.

Apple measured time to first token on a 65,536-token context falling from about 50.5 seconds to 40.6 seconds when it used two cables per link instead of one, per MIXED's Muse Spark report.

Cables are the cheapest speed-up you will ever buy.

LLM Reference lists Kimi K3.1 Pro at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.

Closed frontier models cost far more; DeepSeek's V4-Pro launch price, for example, was reported at roughly a twentieth of Opus 4.7's.

A four-node cluster running Kimi K3.1 Pro generates in the mid-teens of tokens per second per stream, so heavy volume has to be spread across the faster models in the list, such as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, MiniMax M3 and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

The HTML edition of this article in my personal blog includes a calculator so you can plug in your own numbers.

The power-user budget is a ladder. Climb as high as your models need, and no higher.

Sources: the 64 GB Framework price from Notebookcheck's price report and the 128 GB price from Phoronix's Framework coverage; DGX Spark and Mac Studio M5 Max prices from ComputingForGeeks' hardware guide; the AMD Ryzen AI Halo from Tom's Hardware; the 256 GB Mac Studio price is derived from TechRepublic's note that two 256 GB units cost $21,598; RTX PRO 6000 pricing from Tom's DGX Spark launch coverage.

Memory prices have been volatile in 2026, so check before you buy.

If all you need is Qwen3.8-27B, its hosted API costs about $0.20 per million input tokens and $2.50 per million output tokens on LLM Reference.

Light users will never recover a $3,600 machine through token savings alone.

But heavy agentic coders are not light users.

If you push 300 million input tokens and 30 million output tokens a month through a frontier API priced like Kimi K3.1 Pro, that is about $900 a month, and a $3,449 Framework Desktop with 128 GB pays for itself in about four months - provided the local model is good enough for the job.

The real return for power users is not only the money.

It is uncensored models when you need them.

These are the problems I care about most, and they are exactly where cloud AI pricing breaks down.

This section explains why I chose a 2 TB unified memory setup, and why the reason is not chat - it is coordinated teams of 100 or more agents.

Research on open problems is not one clever prompt.

It is thousands of attempts, most of them failures, each re-reading long contexts full of definitions, prior attempts and formal proof states.

When I first wrote this section, I said no AI system had solved a Millennium Prize Problem.

Here is what happened in the autumn of 2026.

Read the dates carefully, because every claim below is still waiting on human review.

The Riemann result had a quieter prelude.

In August, a research version of Claude raised the proven share of zeta zeros on the critical line from 41.6 percent to 67.2 percent, per Anthropic's zeta note - real progress, but not a proof.

The Millennium Prize list on Wikipedia now marks the Riemann Hypothesis and Navier-Stokes as "solution claimed; prize pending".

The Clay Institute has awarded nothing yet, and P vs NP remains open.

Now look at how every one of these results was produced.

That is exactly the workload this section is about.

And ten thousand agents is a cloud bill, not a hobby: at even a tenth of the per-agent token volume I assume below, a swarm that size would cost about $130,000 a day at GPT-5.6 Sol prices (my estimate).

The token volumes are my own planning assumptions; the prices are published list prices.

And that is before prompt caching discounts, retries, failed runs, or the inevitable moment someone leaves a swarm running over a long weekend.

The four-node cluster costs about $96,000 in hardware (see the budget section).

After that, the marginal cost of research is mostly electricity.

Mixed load (estimate): about 1 kW for the cluster, or 8,760 kWh a year - roughly $1,300 a year at $0.15 per kWh, or about ₹70,000 at ₹8 per kWh.

So the first year of local research costs about $100,000 all in, against $1.8 million to $9.1 million for the same token volume in the cloud.

Every year after that costs a few thousand dollars of power.

That is the difference between a research programme you can sustain for a decade and one you can afford for a quarter.

A 100-agent team needs three things at once: strong lead reasoners, fast workers, and room for every agent's working context.

One 512 GB machine forces you to pick one of those.

Here is the memory plan I use for a "swarm" configuration on 2,048 GB:

That leaves roughly 6 GB of working memory per agent for a team of 100, before KV cache quantization stretches it further.

For a "deep" configuration, swap the whole roster for Kimi K3.1 Pro (about 1.56 TB) and run a small team of very strong agents instead.

Is 100 agents realistic on four Mac Studios?

Research agents spend much of their time waiting on tools - Lean proof checks, Python experiments, quantum simulators, literature search - so far fewer than 100 are generating tokens at any instant.

The fast, small-active workers (8B to 16B active for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, 6B for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) carry the volume, and the heavy reasoners are called only when a decision needs them.

Agent swarms at this scale are already real.

Moonshot pushed its Agent Swarm to 300 sub-agents running 4,000 coordinated steps with Kimi K2.6, per a Kimi K2.6 report.

A team of 100 agents without structure is just 100 expensive random walks.

The coordination layer is what turns a swarm into a research group.

Quantum research has its own memory hunger.

A full state-vector simulation stores 2ⁿ complex amplitudes at 16 bytes each:

So a single 512 GB node can hold a 34-qubit state vector with room to spare, while the agent team searches error-correcting codes, circuit compilations and variational ansätze around it.

Tensor-network and stabilizer simulators go much further for structured circuits, and the same agents can write and run them.

Will a 100-agent team on four Mac Studios settle P vs NP?

You would need 10,000+ to 100,000+ agents for that. Maybe even 1 million agents.

But can it solve research level problems for your own company?

I strongly believe the people who make progress on the hardest problems will be the ones who can afford to fail ten thousand times.

Local hardware turns failure from a line item into a habit - and that is how business research and new scientific discoveries have always worked.

AI sovereignty means you, your company or your country can keep using AI on your own terms, no matter what a vendor, a regulator abroad or a supply shock decides.

Owning the weights and the hardware is the most direct way to get there.

It is also the only way to ensure your company is running irrespective of internet outages, natural disasters, international calamities or war.

I am not a lawyer, and you should get legal advice for your jurisdiction.

But I strongly believe that every serious organisation should hold at least one capable model it controls completely.

A local model on a badly managed machine is just a new place for data to leak.

The supply chain is the most overlooked risk.

While researching this article I saw dozens of unofficial re-uploads of flagship models from accounts that have nothing to do with the original labs.

Ransomware is moving laterally through your network.

Your analyst pastes an obfuscated PowerShell loader into an AI assistant and asks what it does.

Safety-tuned models are trained to refuse requests that look like hacking.

The trouble is that defending against an attack looks exactly like studying one.

Those are reasonable choices for public chatbots.

But in an incident room, a false refusal can cost you minutes, and minutes are what separate a contained incident from a company-wide outage.

At the same time, capability is clearly there.

GLM-5.3 scores 84.5 on CyberGym, a vulnerability-discovery benchmark, on its model card.

The knowledge exists inside these models; alignment decides whether your defenders can reach it.

An uncensored local model does all of this without arguing, without sending your malware samples or breach details to a third party, and without a rate limit in the middle of the night.

During a breach, you may not be able to trust your own network, your SaaS accounts or your internet connection.

A model running on an isolated Mac Studio or a disconnected workstation keeps working when everything else is suspect.

And sending live incident data to an external API during a breach is a disclosure decision your legal team should make deliberately - not something an analyst should do at 3 a.m. by accident.

Uncensored models are powerful tools, so treat them like any other powerful tool.

Isolate the machine on a dedicated analysis network with no route to production.

Log every prompt and response for later review.

Write an acceptable-use policy that covers defensive work, authorised testing scope and prohibited uses.

Keep an aligned model for everyone else. The uncensored model belongs in the security toolkit, not on every desk.

Vet the abliterated build using the provenance checklist above.

The community already publishes hundreds of abliterated models, browsable in catalogues such as Featherless's abliterated catalogue, including some aimed at security work, but you must test any such model yourself.

Good news - the defenders now have frontier-grade help that never says no.

Bad news - so do the attackers, which is exactly why your team cannot afford to work with one hand tied behind its back.

Software decides whether you actually enjoy using it.

You just told me a 128 GB box will never pay for itself if I only use Qwen3.8-27B lightly.

You told me a four-node cluster generates Kimi K3.1 Pro at the speed of a fast typist.

Cloud APIs for open models are cheap, they scale instantly, and someone else patches the servers.

With Cloud APIs, I do not need to pay for upgrades and maintenance.

2 TB is overkill for most small businesses.

But cost per token was never the whole story.

You cannot rent sovereignty, you cannot rent an air gap, and you cannot rent a model that will help you dissect ransomware at 3 a.m. without logging your breach on someone else's server.

The same kind of four-Mac Studio cluster that ran Kimi K2 Thinking in late 2025 runs far more capable models today, because the models keep getting more efficient while the hardware you already own stays paid for.

Run the private, sensitive, high-volume and always-on work locally, and keep a cloud API for the rare task that needs the biggest closed model.

Will the cloud API survive a war in your country?

If the AI bubble pops, where will you get your AI?

If all leading AI labs increase costs to cover their bills, what will you do with your current budget?

If your country is listed as opposition to the USA, where is your frontier level AI?

If your company is banned by mistake, what will you do?

If your infrastructure goes down, and you are running a mission-critical business, where is your backup?

If one of your systems are hacked, how will you fight back? Will you feed sensitive company data into foreign servers?

If your system requires cyberattack analysis, how will you bypass safeguards on US AI Companies?

Will you end up sending your sensitive data to Chinese servers, which are regulated by the Chinese government?

These are the reasons why every company on earth needs local LLMs!

Especially in the current geopolitical situation!

Two years ago, running a frontier-class model at home was a stunt.

Four Mac Studios give an enterprise 2,048 GB of unified memory and the freedom to run Kimi K3.1 Pro, GLM-5.3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Inkling 2 Small, Qwen3.8, Mistral Large 4 and Muse Spark Open on its own terms.

A single 64 to 128 GB machine gives a power user Qwen3.8-27B, Inkling 2 Mini, Gemma 4, gpt-oss-120b and Mistral Small 4 - with uncensored builds a download away.

Where will you be when the next price change lands?

Where will you be when the next outage hits?

Where will you be when the next breach starts at 3 a.m.?

The organisations that own their intelligence will move faster, sleep better and defend harder than the ones that rent it.

Especially with uncensored models (with strict access rules!) when cyber-attacks are a real and active threat.

By God's grace, the future of AI is open, local and yours.

And if you are building your AI strategy right now - start with one machine, one model, and one sensitive workflow you will never send to the cloud again.

The best way to build a Local AI system is in modules, one machine at a time, not a big bang!

I am working as a Generative AI Consultant available for work globally, on a remote basis.

I have 500+ publications across 10+ platforms covering AI, agentic systems, quantum computing, LLMs, Local AI, and other emerging technologies, for which I acts as a consultant in Python, Go, Rust, and the Claude AI Ecosystem and the Gemini AI Ecosystem.

Find my work at my personal blog thomascherickal.com and my business consulting website thedigitalfuturist.com.

#9756. Ginger VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?


Ginger VS Grammarly: When it comes to grammar checkers, Ginger and Grammarly are two of the most popular choices on the market. This article aims to highlight the specifics of each one so that you can make a more informed decision about the one you'll use.

What is Grammarly?

If you are a writer, you must have heard of  Grammarly before. Grammarly has over 10M users across the globe, it's probably the most popular AI writing enhancement tool, without a doubt. That's why there's a high chance that you already know about Grammarly.

But today we are going to do a comparison between Ginger and Grammarly, So let's define Grammarly here. Like Ginger, Grammarly is an AI writing assistant that checks for grammatical errors, spellings, and punctuation. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

While the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

Features of Grammarly

  • Grammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve it
  • Create a personal dictionary 
  • Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.
  • Understand inconsistencies. 
  • Detect unclear structure. 
  • Detect Plagiarism.
  • Explore overuse of words and wordiness. 
  • Get to know about the improper tones. 
  • Discover the insensitive language aligns with your intent, audience, style, emotion, and more.


What is Ginger

 Ginger is a writing enhancement tool that not only catches typos and grammatical mistakes but also suggests content improvements. As you type, it picks up on errors then shows you what’s wrong, and suggests a fix. It also provides you with synonyms and definitions of words and allows you to translate your text into dozens of languages.


Ginger Software: Features & Benefits

  • Ginger's software helps you identify and correct common grammatical mistakes, such as consecutive nouns, or contextual spelling correction.
  • The sentence rephrasing feature can help you convey your meaning perfectly.
  • Ginger acts like a personal coach that helps you practice certain exercises based on your mistakes.
  • The dictionary feature helps users understand the meanings of words.

In addition, the program provides a text reader, so you can gauge your writing’s conversational tone.


Ginger vs Grammarly

Grammarly and Ginger are two popular grammar checker software brands that help you to become a better writer. But if you’re undecided about which software to use, consider these differences:

  • Grammarly only supports the English language while Ginger supports 40+ languages.
  • Grammarly offers a wordiness feature while Ginger lacks a Wordiness feature.
  • Grammarly shows an accuracy score while Ginger lacks an accuracy score feature.
  • Grammarly has a plagiarism checker while ginger doesn't have such a feature.
  • Grammarly can recognize an incorrect use of numbers while Ginger can’t recognize an incorrect use of numbers.
  • Grammarly and Ginger both have mobile apps.
  • Ginger and Grammarly offer monthly, quarterly, and annual plans.
  • Grammarly allows you to check uploaded documents. while Ginger doesn't check uploaded documents.
  • Grammarly Offers a tone suggestion feature while Ginger doesn't offer a tone suggestion feature.
  • Ginger helps to translate documents into 40+ languages while Grammarly doesn't have a translation feature.
  • Ginger Offers text to speech features while Grammarly doesn't have such features.


Grammarly Score: 7/10

Ginger:4/10

So Grammarly  wins here.

Ginger VS Grammarly: Pricing Difference

  • Ginger offers a Premium subscription for 13.99$/month. it comes at $11.19/month for quarterly and $7.49/month for an annual subscription with 40$ off.
  • On the other hand,  Grammarly offers a Premium subscription for $30/month for a monthly plan  $20/month for quarterly, and $12/month for an annual subscription.

For companies with three or more employees, the Business plan costs $12.50/month for each member of your team. 

Ginger Wins Here

Ginger vs Grammarly – Pros and Cons


Grammarly Pros

  • Offers  free version
  • All-in-one tool (grammar checker + spell checker + punctuation checker)
  • Allows you to edit a document without affecting the formatting.
  • Style checker (paid version)

  • Active and passive voice checker
  • Personal dictionary 
  • Plagiarism checker (paid version)
  • Available on all major devices and platforms
  • Free mobile apps 
  • User-friendly interface
  • Browser extensions and MS word add-ons
  • Can upload and download documents


Grammarly Cons

  • Supports only English 
  • Customer support only via email
  • Limits to 150,000 words
  • Subscription plans can be a bit pricey 
  • Doesn’t offer a free trial
  • No refund policy

Ginger Pros

  • Offers free version
  • All-in-one tool (grammar checker + spell checker + punctuation checker)
  • Affordable Subscription plans (Additionals discounts are available)
  • Active and passive voice changer
  • Translates documents in 40+ languages 
  • Personal dictionary
  • Browser extension available 
  •  Personal trainers help clients develop their knowledge of grammar.
  • Text-to-speech feature reads work out loud
  • Get a full refund within 7 days


Ginger Cons

  • Mobile apps aren't free
  • Limited monthly corrections for free users
  • No style checker
  • No plagiarism checker
  • Not as user-friendly as Grammarly
  • You are unable to upload or download documents; however, you may copy and paste files as needed.
  • Doesn't offer a free trial


Summarizing the Ginger VS Grammarly: My Recommendation

While both writing assistants are fantastic in their ways, you need to choose the one you want. 

For example, go for Grammarly if you want a plagiarism tool included. 

Choose Ginger if you want to write in languages other than English. I will to the differences for you in order to make the distinctions clearer.

  • Grammarly offers a plagiarism checking tool
  • Ginger provides text to speech tool
  • Grammarly helps you check uploaded documents
  • Ginger supports over 40 languages
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX
Both Ginger and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. Depending on your needs, you might want to use Ginger over Grammarly. As per my experience, I found Grammarly easier to use than Ginger.

Which one you like let me know in the comments section also give your opinions in the comments section below.

#9755. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

#9754. China's 'Armory Castle' Lays Siege to VMware vCenter Zero-Day

During the last wave of major VMware vCenter security updates, a China-nexus threat group likely already had its next zero-day up its sleeve.

Chinese state-sponsored hackers have been using a newly disclosed VMware zero-day vulnerability and an array of custom malware to compromise victims' virtualization stacks for several months.

In October, Mandiant described a campaign by China's Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) to exploit organizations through BeyondTrust's Remote Support tool. The group used a zero-day to breach the edge appliance, then stole credentials and secrets useful for network reconnaissance and downstream compromises within organizations. Exactly what that downstream compromise looked like, though, was unclear at the time.

It appears now that BeyondTrust was merely an entrée to a deeper, more interesting, and much more complex campaign. In a follow-up blog post this week, Mandiant researchers described a chained attack beginning with BeyondTrust, moving through obscure Linux appliances, and landing on VMware technologies, at which point the attackers utilized another zero-day and more than half a dozen malware programs to totally undress their targets' virtual machine (VM) environments.

Related:Cyprus Becomes Espionage Target for Iranian Hackers

That zero-day has only now come to light, months since China first exploited it. In a security advisory, VMware owner Broadcom recommended that customers update their systems. Tracked as CVE-2026-123890, the vulnerability allows for authentication bypass in VMware vCenter and earned a "critical" 9.8 out of 10 score in the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS).

From tagged Remote Support boxes, Mandiant observed Armory Castle scanning a victim's internal environment, looking for open ports associated with VMware.

Instead of going for the goods immediately, the group established forward operating bases inside other, possibly unrelated Linux appliances in the same network. These appliances lacked endpoint detection and response (EDR) visibility, allowing the group to establish persistence and stage its malware arsenal away from the parts of the network where defenders were looking. Among other malware, it was there that Armory Castle deployed "Bonesaw," a Go-based remote exploitation tool customized for vCenter.

The VMware vCenter Server is the central control plane used to manage multiple VMs and their ESXi hosts. Because it oversees everything else, few technologies are more useful for lateral movement, ransomware attacks, etc., than vCenter is. It's why this summer, the disclosure of two critical vCenter vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-59309 and CVE-2026-59310, caused a stir.

Related:Latin America Sees Cyberattacks on Ports, Pipelines & Manufacturing

While organizations were rushing to patch the two vCenter vulnerabilities known to Broadcom, Armory Castle appears to have had an extra one up its sleeve. In September, it was able to use Bonesaw against a victim that had already patched its vCenter; Bonesaw was tuned to exploit CVE-2026-123890, a flaw that stems from the vCenter login system's use of predictable, time-based UUIDv1 timestamp generation in Secure Remote Password (SRP) authentication handling.

Exploiting CVE-2026-123890 afforded Armory Castle a shared session key it could use to create new authenticated sessions as an administrator, bypassing the normal authentication process entirely. Bonesaw then paid more dividends, automating the process of copying vCenter's internal directory database and creating powerful new accounts for further damage.

At this point, Armory Castle had total control over the victim's vCenter. Yet it continued on with machine-like focus; the attackers deployed a tool called "Sawsnake" to turn the Bonesaw-stolen vCenter login-signing key into forged authentication tokens, bypassing multifactor authentication (MFA) and enabling impersonation of any user. It then jumped to ESXi hypervisors and found and extracted system files.

For high-risk organizations, updating VMware instances to patched versions can't be the end of the story.

Related:AI Agents Zip From Flaw Discovery to Root Access in 11 Minutes

Because vCenter is just so sensitive, Mandiant urged organizations not to rely solely on patching known vulnerabilities as they come up. It pointed to its vSphere Defender's Guide, published earlier this spring. Its recommendations include the standard fare — promptly updating and isolating management systems, encrypting particularly sensitive systems, and applying especially tight controls to administrator accounts — but also offers more pointed items. It notes that vCenter doesn't necessarily record all important operating system (OS) activity, and that sophisticated attackers can delete local logs post-compromise; therefore, organizations should consider forwarding logs to a separate security information and event management (SIEM) platform.

Mandiant researchers also advised that organizations not rely on vCenter's built-in firewall, as it has too many limitations. For example, it doesn't generate remote logs for rejected connection attempts or certain shell activity, doesn't enforce policies for data egress, and, most of all, it's simply at risk for being built into the very system it's designed to secure.

"Organizations must adopt a proactive, Zero Trust approach to infrastructure hardening to defend against current and undiscovered zero-day vulnerabilities," the researchers wrote.

#9753. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

#9752. How Security Vendors Are Tackling Access-Control Challenges for AI Agents

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Identity, runtime, and development controls are converging as enterprises look for ways to keep agents within their assigned jobs. But vendors' approaches vary, so CISOs face a choice.

As organizations expand their use of artificial intelligence (AI) agents to perform tasks traditionally done by employees, security teams must control not only which systems agents can access but which actions they are authorized to take.

The Blueprint Alliance, an industry group advocating for coordinated controls, notes that 92% of organizations use autonomous AI agents, but only 34% secure them with the same rigor as they do for human users.

Many vendors have begun adding capabilities to better control agents. Their approaches overlap, leaving CISOs to determine how the new offerings fit into a coherent security architecture that keeps agents focused on their assigned tasks and prevents overpermissioning machine identities beyond what their human users can access.

Earlier this month, CrowdStrike introduced what it calls an AI Kill Switch, which gives security teams a way to block an agent's access to AI models via connected gateways. The AI Kill Switch, launched during CrowdStrike's Fal.Con Europe conference in Barcelona, extends Falcon Guardian, the AI detection and response offering that supports Windows, macOS, and Linux endpoints. Guardian discovers agents and controls which ones may run and connects prompts, identities, tool calls, and skills to downstream actions in an execution graph.

Related:Phishing-Resistant Isn't Enough; Yubico Takes Aim at Identity-Verification Gap

The kill switch works with CrowdStrike's Falcon AI Gateway or connected third-party gateways. Its current enforcement point is model access, rather than every system an agent can reach. CrowdStrike says it will later extend the capability to terminate agent processes and revoke their access to enterprise resources.

"The hardest case is the agent that behaves abnormally without breaking a business process rule," CrowdStrike's chief product officer AJ Shipley said during an Oct. 29 media roundtable discussion.

Discussing agent insider threat detection, Shipley described an approach that establishes a baseline of expected agent and user behavior and then detects deviations, even when no explicit policy violation occurs.

CrowdStrike also announced earlier this month agreements to acquire two startups — Fiddler AI and Dreadnode — extending its push into agent observability and predeployment security testing. Fiddler evaluates agents and helps explain their behavior in production, while Dreadnode tests models, applications, and agents for security weaknesses before deployment. The Wall Street Journal reported a combined purchase price of approximately $495 million. The acquisitions have not yet closed.

Related:Cyera's Oasis Security Buy Is All About AI Agent Control

CrowdStrike is one of several vendors addressing agent access controls. Anaconda is combining agentic software development with autonomous security testing, Cisco and Teleport are tying access to infrastructure identity, Okta is enforcing identity policy when agents call tools, and Fortinet is extending controls over execution and application behavior.

Anaconda, for instance, is approaching the problem through application development by pairing agentic software development with autonomous security testing. Last month, it expanded its AI Dev Factory, combining development agent swarms with autonomous red-team agents that probe models, agents, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for weaknesses. The release incorporates technology from Anaconda's August acquisition of Enkrypt AI, supporting red teaming across more than 300 attack categories and runtime guardrails that approve, modify, or block risky behavior.

Anaconda's earlier acquisitions of Outerbounds, Kilo Code, and Enkrypt AI collectively bring together production orchestration, agentic development, and AI security.

"Our road map out for all three acquisitions would have been about two or three years’ worth of engineering effort," Anaconda CEO David DeSanto says, describing Enkrypt as the final component needed to accomplish this goal.

Related:USA Fencing Lunges Into the Hidden Identity Challenge in Amateur Sports

Testing agents is one requirement; limiting their authority in production is another. Cisco is approaching that problem through infrastructure identity, becoming Teleport's largest strategic investor in August. Teleport's open source platform replaces passwords and permanent SSH keys with ephemeral certificates.

Teleport CEO Ev Kontsevoy describes an incident in which a customer deployed an agent to process data and update a database. When the intended database became unavailable, the agent found another and tried to update it. The agent was trying to complete its assignment rather than respond to an attacker. Its improvisation nevertheless exposed the difference between granting access and containing behavior.

"Would you say it's a security accident or what? Whatever it is, it's terrifying when it happens, particularly at scale," Kontsevoy tells Dark Reading.

Cisco and Teleport's partnership addresses containment through verified infrastructure identities and access granted "just in time, just enough," says Peter Bailey, Cisco's senior VP and general manager for security.

"We want to be able to take action and stop action based upon identity," Bailey says.

On Oct. 26, Cisco introduced Privileged Infrastructure Access, applying the partnership's infrastructure-identity approach to administrators and agents. Cisco says it provides temporary, identity-bound access to network infrastructure, records sessions, and ends privileges when the task is complete.

Kontsevoy describes attaching privileges to tasks rather than permanently assigning them to accounts. A deployment ticket could identify the engineer, laptop, and CI/CD pipeline involved. Each is granted necessary privileges, which disappear when the ticket closes. Teleport's MCP gateway also enforces policy and tracks relationships among initiating actors, agents, and subagents, he says.

When an agent acts on an employee's behalf, controls must distinguish the agent's permissions from those of the person directing the agent to avoid inappropriate privilege escalation.

Consider a scenario in which an HR assistant runs on a service account that can read every employee record. A contractor asking the agent for the CEO's compensation could get the response since the assistant has access the contractor doesn't. According to Okta, this agent would be a "confused deputy," as it exercises authority the requester lacks.

To address this scenario, Okta's Agent Gateway treats agents as "first-class" identities; it preserves the distinction between their permissions and those of the users directing them. It requires a credential that identifies both the user and the agent and uses token exchange to preserve the delegation context. The gateway limits the tools available, while the downstream MCP server enforces the user's record-level access. Agent Gateway is now generally available as an addition to AI agents, an identity-security offering made generally available in April.

In an Oct. 8 blog post, Okta described plans for Cross App Access support and a gateway-based kill switch. Officials said the latter "will make agent deactivation immediate, down to tokens already issued, by rejecting any request carrying a token issued to a deactivated agent."

Okta is not alone in extending identity controls to agents. At its Fal.Con conference in Las Vegas in September, CrowdStrike announced Agentic Identity Provider, designed to establish trusted agent identities, broker time-limited access, and link actions to initiating employees or systems.

Microsoft is pursuing a related approach through Project Perception, connecting agent identity, behavioral risk signals, and access controls across its security products via its new Guardian Agent capabilities.

Meanwhile, Fortinet is extending AI inspection across its existing network security products. Last month, the company announced the FortiGuard Inline AI Security Service for FortiGate customers and described expanded FortiAIGate capabilities incorporating Virtue AI technology, which Fortinet acquired earlier this year. Virtue AI adds policy-derived guardrails, continuous assessment, code analysis, and agent red teaming.

Fortinet executive vice president Anthony James describes more than 50 simulated application environments in which customers can test agent boundaries before connecting to real systems. He says Virtue can block an agent from communicating with MCP tools or servers not approved for its task and detect prompt sequences that progress from innocuous to malicious.

FortiAIGate began by monitoring communications to and from AI infrastructure, James adds. Customers deploying agents sought a deeper understanding of the application. Models, MCP servers, agents, and skills "require a little deeper application knowledge than just interpreting the network traffic," he says.

Overlapping approaches have prompted coordination efforts. In September, Okta announced the Blueprint Alliance with vendors including AWS, CrowdStrike, Google Cloud, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Zscaler. The group aims to develop a shared architecture for securing agents across vendors' products.

The alliance has outlined principles for agent identity, task-scoped access, monitoring, and containment. Whether those principles translate into interoperable products and expanded adoption remains to be seen.

Taken together, these approaches point to a common requirement: keeping an agent's access tied to its assigned task. Identity verification, security testing, and runtime monitoring address different parts of that requirement, but no single control confirms that an agent will remain within its assignment.

Emerging control planes aim to connect those controls across tools and systems — limiting agents to their assigned tasks rather than letting AI software determine how far its authority extends.

Jeff has contributed to Dark Reading since 2022 and has written for Channel Futures for over five years. Before launching his freelance career, he was an editor at 1105 Media, where he served as editor-in-chief of Redmond magazine and contributed to its sister publications, including Redmond Channel Partner, Application Development Trends, and Virtualization Review.

Previously, Jeff held editorial roles at CMP Media’s CommunicationsWeek, InternetWeek, and VARBusiness.
