#9739. Who Was Hermes Trismegistus, and Why Does He Still Matter?

Design engineer, AI product engineer and founder of Lunar Computing. I build products and write about the decisions underneath them.

Design engineer, AI product engineer and founder of Lunar Computing. I build products and write about the decisions underneath them.

Design engineer, AI product engineer and founder of Lunar Computing. I build products and write about the decisions underneath them.

Every path in my MA led back to one figure, and the figure was not historical.

The Corpus Hermeticum, the sub-lunar sphere, the seven planetary spheres, the idea that nothing dies but dissolves and recombines, the claim that the cosmos was thought into being before it was made. All of it is attributed to a man called Hermes Trismegistus. Hermes Thrice-Greatest. And when you try to find the man, he is not there.

There are three different answers to the question of who Hermes Trismegistus was, and all three were taken seriously at different points in history.

The first answer is that he was a real Egyptian sage, a contemporary or near-contemporary of Moses, who wrote down the wisdom of the gods. This is what Renaissance humanists believed when they rediscovered the texts in the fifteenth century. Marsilio Ficino translated the Corpus Hermeticum into Latin in 1463 for Cosimo de' Medici, interrupting his translation of Plato because his patron thought the Hermetica was older and therefore more important. Cosimo turned out to be wrong about the dating. The Hermetica ended up shaping Renaissance thought anyway.

The second answer is that he was a later composite, a syncretic figure that emerged when Greek and Egyptian religion fused in Alexandria. The Greek god Hermes, messenger and guide of souls, was identified with the Egyptian god Thoth, scribe of the gods and inventor of writing. Thrice-Greatest is a title that belongs to Thoth in earlier Egyptian texts. The merging happened somewhere between the founding of Alexandria in 331 BCE and the collation of the surviving Hermetic corpus in the second and third centuries CE. No single person wrote the Corpus Hermeticum. A tradition wrote it, over generations, under one name.

The third answer is the one the texts themselves give. The Hermetica presents Hermes not as a historical person at all, but as a stand-in for divine intelligence writing through human hands. In that reading the question of who wrote it is the wrong question. The point is that the ideas are not the property of any individual.

The first answer is wrong. The second is almost certainly correct. The third is the one the texts insist on.

Eighteen books, of which seventeen survive. Book Fifteen is lost. The surviving texts were collated in Alexandria in the second and third centuries CE, written in Greek, Latin and Coptic. Not in the hieroglyphs you might expect of something claiming Egyptian origin. The translation into English I worked from most often was John Everard's 1650 version, which has an archaic cadence you can almost hear when you read it out loud:

Atum is the central figure of the cosmology. Atum is the cosmic mind, the pre-existing intelligence that contains all potential. The word itself is older than the Hermetic texts; it belongs to ancient Egyptian religion, where Atum was the self-created god of Heliopolis. The Hermetic writers inherit the name and keep most of its original meaning. Atum is the first thing that existed. Atum is the totality of everything that exists. Atum is not a person.

From Atum comes everything, through thought. The physical universe is not primary. Matter is not the foundation. Thought is the foundation, and matter is what thought produces when it slows down enough to become form. This is what the Hermetic phrase light precipitates matter actually means. Light, in the Hermetic sense, is not photons. It is the intelligence of the cosmos, from which matter crystallises as the expression of thought taking shape.

Thoth was the Egyptian god of writing, wisdom, measurement, time, and the moon. He mediated between worlds and wrote the words of magic that structured reality. Hermes was the Greek god of crossings, boundaries, messages, and guides. Hermes psychopompos is the one who escorts souls across the threshold of death.

When the two merged, what emerged was a figure who was simultaneously the source of all written knowledge and the guide across the threshold of death. This is not a small coincidence. The Hermetic corpus is fundamentally about crossings: between the known and the unknowable, the living and the dead, the material and the immaterial. The figure who authored it had to be able to stand in both worlds at once.

Mead, in his 1906 translation, put it precisely:

Inner Reason. That phrase is the whole thing. The claim embedded in the Thoth-Hermes synthesis is that the same intelligence which governs the structure of the cosmos also governs the structure of law, language, measurement, and thought. The writer of the universe is the writer of grammar.

The Hermetica is explicit that death is not what it appears to be.

Read slowly. Dissolution is not death. The physical form disperses. The arrangement of matter changes. But nothing that was there is gone, because the matter itself was only a temporary form. What survives is what was always primary: the thought, the pattern, the intelligence that gathered the matter into a shape in the first place.

This is not a religious claim about an afterlife. It is a cosmological claim about what kind of thing a thing is. For the Hermetic writers, everything in the physical world is a local, temporary expression of a thought in Atum's mind. When the local form dissipates, the thought does not. The universe is not made of objects. It is made of acts of thinking, with objects as their residue.

I built a cube. I painted quotes on its fabric walls in ultraviolet paint. I lit it with LEDs. I filmed the inside with six GoPros to make a 360-degree video you could enter through a VR headset. The whole project was an argument that reality depends on what you can perceive, and that what you can perceive is a tiny fraction of what exists.

The Corpus Hermeticum says the same thing, earlier and more seriously. The visible spectrum is one sliver of electromagnetic radiation. The physical body is one expression of consciousness. The seven classical planets are one layer of a cosmological system that keeps going beyond them. In every direction, the Hermetica says: what you can see is evidence of something larger that you cannot.

Hermes Trismegistus is the name we put on the claim that the larger thing is legible. That reality is not only accessible to the senses, which know very little, but to the mind, which can read the structure of the cosmos the way a scribe reads a scroll. That the universe is authored, not accidental. Whether or not you accept the claim, the claim itself is the foundation of every Western esoteric tradition that follows. Neoplatonism inherits it. The Renaissance inherits it. Jung inherits it. Most of what we now call symbolic or archetypal thinking traces back, eventually, to a nobody called Thrice-Greatest writing under an Egyptian name in a Greek city.

I did not come out of the MA believing Hermes Trismegistus was real in the way that Moses was. I came out of it believing he was real in the way that Sherlock Holmes is real. He is the voice through which a particular way of reading the cosmos was kept alive for two thousand years, across cultures and languages, intact enough that an undergraduate could find him in a library and understand him.

The next piece in this series looks at what that cosmology actually says about mythology: the planetary gods, the Saturn-Jupiter lineage, and why Greek myth reads differently once you know it is cosmological instruction in disguise.

This is part 4 of A Journey Through Light.

#9738. Industrial Serial Gateways Broadcast That They're Insecure

Critical OT access devices will often tell you, and anyone else, whether they're protected by authentication — and many aren't.

Internet scans indicate that some substantial fraction of serial device servers deployed at operational technology (OT) sites worldwide not only lack authentication but also broadcast the fact publicly.

We all have a friend or a family member who's deeply insecure, and it's obvious as soon as they start talking. The same can be said of serial-to-IP gateways. Recently, Adrian Cheek, senior cybercrime researcher for Flare, probed the wider Internet for these sorts of devices, finding that a substantial chunk of them are discoverable. Worse, they often responded to straightforward requests by saying whether they were or were not protected by authentication — and many were not.

An insecure serial-to-IP gateway is a serious risk to anyone downstream of it. These devices are responsible for translating information between the Internet and industrial machinery. So in a cyberattack, a reachable and unauthenticated one can inadvertently translate an Internet-based threat into one that affects major, safety-critical machines.

Related:How to Assess OT Incident Response Preparedness

Using a specific vendor's UDP discovery service, rather than probing all vendors' devices, Cheek found 2,474 serial-to-IP gateways exposed on the Web. They seemed to map to real devices rather than honeypots, with half of them located in Russia.

For some reason, in response to the researcher's unsolicited probes, around half of the devices — 1,265 — proffered their authentication status. Of those that did, 973 reported that authentication was disabled. In other words, 39.3% of all Internet-exposed gateways visibly lacked authentication, and among those whose status could be gleaned, that figure was 77%.

"These devices ship with authentication off. An integrator sets one up on a bench, gets the meter or the drive or the Remote Terminal Unit (RTU) talking to the SCADA host, and moves on to the next site," Cheek laments. "The device then does one job for 10 or 15 years, and nobody logs into it again. In many cases, the operator doesn't even know it exists because it went in as part of someone else's equipment."

There are also understandable, if not entirely justifiable, reasons why operators fail to conceal and lock down their serial device servers. Cheek cites a multitude of reasons, including that enabling such security features can break software on the host side.

"Older SCADA packages and virtual serial port drivers may not support the secured modes, so an operator who switches them on can lose the link to the field," he says. "Then someone has to drive to an unstaffed site to fix it. Firmware updates carry the same risk at a remote site with no spare on hand. People who have been burned by that once are slow to touch a working device again."

Related:Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast

Still, an exposed, unauthenticated serial gateway is a welcome mat for bad actors. Not only does it give arbitrary actors entry into sensitive OT systems and eliminate the need to exploit any kind of vulnerabilities, it also allows attackers to use the vendor's own supplied tools, which could blend malicious activity in with normal IT-OT traffic.

Cheek made special mention of the risk to mobile network operators and, even more specifically, private access point name (APN) service providers. Last year's Polish power grid attack used a private APN to pivot from a wind farm's network to the power plant where the attackers ultimately shut down a steam turbine, water treatment system, and seven serial-to-IP devices. According to Flare, 322 of the 2,474 discovered devices in the study lived in address space associated with known mobile network operators in Europe and the Middle East.

OT operators can begin to secure their OT access layer by first doing an inventory of the devices they're running. "For every cellular unit, find out what plan the SIM is on and whether it gets a public address. Then ask your carrier in writing whether devices on your private network can reach each other or devices belonging to other customers," Cheek notes. "Don't assume the managed product isolates them. In the Polish incident, that missing isolation is what let the attacker move between two unrelated organizations."

Related:Fresh European Fridge Attacks Put Cold-Chain Security in Focus

Next, he advises, "Lock down the data ports as well as the login. Most of these devices let you restrict which IP addresses can open a connection. Configure them so only the SCADA host can reach the serial ports and only an engineering workstation can reach the management interface. Switch off the services you don't use, which on most units means the discovery service, Telnet, older SNMP, and often the Web interface. Remove SSH and Telnet entirely from anything that faces the carrier network," and plop a strict firewall between the gateway and control network.

There are also general practices organizations can put in place, like ensuring that the next time they purchase serial device servers, a person or team is assigned to be responsible for the devices, and that they have necessary credentials, configuration, and network details from system integrators.

At the end of the day, though, nothing compares to preventing an attacker's ability to find and speak to a device in the first place.

"Even a fully patched gateway with authentication on is usually connected to equipment on the serial side that has no security of its own," Cheek points out. "A meter, a drive, or an RTU will accept any correctly formed command that reaches it. So the useful question is who can reach the gateway at all, because whoever can reach it gets whatever is behind it. Authentication and patching both matter, but restricting what can reach the gateway does more good than either."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9737. Decision Models in Hugging Face

Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:

"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

This is the key idea behind decision models.

A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models)

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:

We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:

A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

A decision model request has the following two components:

The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z1,…,zKz_1,\ldots,z_Kz1​,…,zK​, (with KKK classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:

pi=exp⁡(zi)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​

∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​

In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

The model again produces a probability distribution:

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable XXX representing the level, the expectation is:

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​

E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7

This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p)

P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

For a Choice with KKK options, the confidence is:

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​

where pmax⁡p_{\max}pmax​ is the largest predicted probability.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998:

C=3(0.998)−12=0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C=23(0.998)−1​=0.997

Notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

Transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:

Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:

The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:

We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter:

First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

Great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that says whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.

I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.

Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator

For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?

"Not because x, but because y" is very AI-sloppy language.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface.

Nobody thinks that, literally. What I mean by that is, nothing capable of thinking would have written this sentence down because no thinking entity would suspect that decision models originated probabilistic classification. Only a non-thinking source of language, such as an LLM, might generate this sentence.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Again, nobody thinks that, meaning only an LLM might generate this sentence.

The state + questions interface carries over to hosted decision models too. meraGPT Decider 1.1 takes the same shape through an API (model decider-1.1) rather than as open weights: up to 255 options per choice question, images in the state, and if you offer an "I don't know" option it takes it when the state doesn't support an answer. Against TypeSafe Jev 1.14 on the same items it's ahead on typed decisions, calibration and large label sets. Input is $0.04 per million tokens and output is free.

Release notes: https://meragpt.com/blog/introducing-decider-1-1?utm_source=huggingface&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=hf_decision_blog

#9736. Your AI Is Generating PRs, Not ROI

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

AI coding tools are generating more pull requests than ever, but more PRs don't equal ROI unless that code ships, holds up in production and reduces work downstream.

Ask any engineering leader if their team uses AI to write code, and you'll get a yes before you finish the question. Ask them what that AI is worth, and watch the yes turn into a pause.

That pause is the actual state of the industry right now. Not "should we adopt AI." That question is over. The question nobody has a good answer to is simpler and more uncomfortable: can you prove it worked?

We talk to a lot of engineering leaders whose teams have already bought the AI. Vendors, internal agents, standardized copilots, all of it. And when we ask how they know it's paying off, we hear some version of the same three things, over and over, from companies that have nothing else in common.

Here's the accepted story: AI writes code faster, so engineering gets faster, so the org gets more done. It's clean. It's also wrong, or at least wrong enough to be dangerous.

Speed of code generation isn't the same thing as speed of value delivery. We've heard this described, almost word for word, by leaders at very different companies: their AI tooling is optimized for the speed of the coding loop, and that optimization is flooding review queues with pull requests that don't address the problems actually costing them money. One technology leader we spoke with put a number on it: their organization still allocates 30 to 40 percent of R&D to legacy sustenance. An AI that makes commits faster doesn't touch that number. It might make it worse, because now there's more code to sustain.

More code, faster, is a vanity metric. It looks like progress on a dashboard. It is not the same thing as fewer defects, fewer escalations, less tech debt, or a codebase anyone actually trusts. If your only instrumented signal is "how fast did we ship the diff," you've measured the part of the SDLC that was never the bottleneck.

The more sophisticated a team gets with AI, the worse this problem gets, not better. We talked with a leader at an enterprise planning-software company who had built dozens of finance agents and an internal factory that turns specs directly into agents. Real infrastructure, real investment. And their honest assessment was that they have no standardized way to measure how their engineers actually use these tools, and now they're dealing with agent sprawl: agents triggering each other, versioning headaches, token spend nobody forecasted, and a growing need to gate daisy-chained agents just to protect the budget and the systems underneath them. This team caps R&D spend as a percentage of revenue and wants AI to bring that number down every year. Nobody can currently tell them if it is.

That's not a failure of ambition. It's a failure of measurement discipline arriving after the infrastructure, instead of before it.

We heard the same shape of problem from a team running a home-grown AI development process, stitched together across a project tracker, a code host, an LLM, and a browser-automation tool for execution. It works, in the sense that a demo works. But their own words to me were that the current evaluation criteria are largely subjective, and what they actually want is a clean, quantifiable way to tell the business whether the tooling is worth what it costs. A demo is not a metric. A vibe is not ROI.

There's a second version of this problem that shows up earlier in the buying process. Teams benchmark every new AI purchase against the general-purpose AI they already pay for. We've had conversations where the honest pushback was some version of: our senior engineers already get most of what they need from existing docs and the chat assistant they use every day, so why would we pay for something else? That's a fair question, and it's one every vendor in this category, including us, has to answer with evidence, not adjectives.

None of this is a story about bad tools. Cursor-style coding assistants, general chat assistants, internal agent factories: they're all doing exactly what they were built to do, which is help someone write code faster. The gap isn't in the tool. It's in the fact that "wrote code faster" was never the metric that mattered, and almost nobody instrumented the metric that does.

If speed of code generation is the wrong number, what's the right one? It's the same handful of things it's always been, just harder to see once agents are shipping code faster than anyone can review it by hand: defects that never reach production. Tickets that never escalate to L3. Tech debt that shrinks instead of compounding. Time to root cause. Time to trust a change before it ships.

Those aren't vibes. They're measurable — but only by something that holds your code, your production behavior, and what your customers actually report in one model instead of three disconnected tools. That's the argument for an engineering world model: not more code, but a traceable line from every change to its consequence, and the judgment to tell you which one you're looking at. Code simulations exist for the same reason: catching the defect before it merges is worth more than shipping the diff a day earlier. Agentic debugging is worth more than agentic writing, because writing was never the expensive part of the SDLC. Understanding what you wrote always was.

We break down the metrics that belong in front of your board, including MTTR, defect escape rate, escalation frequency, and engineering capacity reclaimed, in The Engineering Leader’s Operational Guide to Compounding ROI with AI.

The teams we talked with weren't wrong to adopt AI. They were wrong about which loop to speed up. Every engineering org we know is currently running an experiment on itself, at scale, with no control group and no instrumentation. Fix the instrumentation before you fix the model. The PRs were never the point.

Want to see how much engineering capacity your team could recover with a multiplayer platform? Run your numbers with PlayerZero's AI ROI calculator.

#9735. Top 10 Best PLR(Private Label Rights) Websites | Which One You Should Join in 2022?



Content creation is one of the biggest struggles for many marketers and business owners. It often requires both time and financial resources, especially if you plan to hire a writer.
Today, we have a fantastic opportunity to use other people's products by purchasing Private Label Rights.

#9734. How Southeastern University Got a Handle on Its Data

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Data security posture management (DSPM) allowed the university to uncover sensitive information, tighten access controls, and lay the groundwork for safer AI adoption.

Southeastern University had a data security problem hiding in plain sight. Like many universities, it operated a sprawling IT environment in which individual departments maintained their own workflows and data repositories. Student records, financial information, and other personally identifiable information (PII) were scattered across file servers, Google Drive, Microsoft OneDrive, SharePoint, databases, and other systems. The university had no reliable way to see what sensitive data it held, where it was stored, whose information it contained, or who could access it.

The challenge is not unique to Southeastern. A 2024 Kiteworks survey of higher education institutions found that nearly half of respondents (49%) used five or more tools to send and share sensitive information. Just 19% said they could track and control sensitive data shared internally, and only 14% could do so when information was exchanged externally.

Related:Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls

While Kiteworks' study found the education sector to be at considerably higher risk than other sectors, its more recent 2026 survey suggests the problem extends well beyond higher education. Among 450 security, compliance, and technology professionals surveyed across industries, 54% said their organizations used four or more separate platforms to exchange sensitive information, 73% had no enforcement restricting which of those channels employees could use, and just 39% validated their sensitive data on a quarterly or more frequent basis. The findings highlight the challenges organizations face in maintaining visibility and control of sensitive information across increasingly complex IT environments.

"We knew there was a lot of data out there, but we didn't know exactly what it was or where it lived," Rhoden says. "Our data was kind of spread across diverse areas, and it basically created a challenge for us to have visibility across all of that."

Related:Getting Past the Post-Quantum Cryptography Discovery Phase

The university initially relied on discovery and security features built into platforms such as Google Workspace and Microsoft 365. But looking at each environment separately made it difficult to develop a comprehensive picture of the university's data and the protections around it. It was harder to tell who had access to sensitive information or when sensitive data was exported and shared without necessary protections. Meanwhile, growing AI adoption across campus was creating new concerns about how employees and other users accessed, shared, and handled sensitive information.

As a small private university in Lakeland, Fla., Southeastern's IT team didn't have the resources to manually discover, classify, and govern data across all these environments. So a little over a year ago, Rhoden began looking for a data security posture management (DSPM) platform that could automate much of that work and give his team a clearer picture of the university's exposure.

After evaluating at least three DSPM products, Southeastern selected Lightbeam's Data Identity Graph because the data engine could consider the broader context when identifying sensitive information, rather than relying primarily on predefined keywords and patterns. Other evaluated products generated too many false positives when they flagged information based on superficial similarities to sensitive data. Lightbeam's approach resulted in fewer false positives, he says.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

Southeastern connected Lightbeam to its Microsoft and Google environments, file servers, databases, email systems, and other repositories. The platform uses APIs and purpose-built connectors to link these disparate sources, scan information where it resides, and identify and classify sensitive data. This meant the university could gain a unified view of its data across its environment without moving all of it into a centralized repository.

One particularly difficult part of the process was determining when records across different systems referred to the same person.

"How do we link the user in a database for our student information system to that same user in Google Workspace and Microsoft 365, so that we get the full picture that the entity is the same person across all those different sources?" Rhoden says, noting that was one of the biggest deployment challenges the security team faced.

Lightbeam also helped the university develop more granular categories for information, such as academic records, student financial aid, loans, tuition, and FAFSA records. This allowed Rhoden's team to distinguish among different types of sensitive information and apply more appropriate access, retention, and compliance policies.

"If files are being shared internally within a department, they should be shared in a designated location," Rhoden says, by way of an example. "If they're being shared internally within SEU, they should be shared in another designated location. And if they're being shared externally, there's a specific process to follow."

The deployment has given Southeastern visibility into more than 180TB of data, encompassing 7.6 million files across 13 data sources. Lightbeam identified 642,000 files containing sensitive information and helped the university associate that information with approximately 1.7 million individual and organizational identities, Rhoden says.

The improved visibility has already helped the university identify files and cloud links that were accessible to more people than necessary. That has given the IT team a basis for tightening permissions and moving toward least-privilege access. Southeastern has also established baseline policies for identifying externally exposed information and data that no longer needs to be retained. The next step is to implement more automated access and retention controls, including safeguards for the sensitive information that AI applications can access.

That last area, in particular, is becoming increasingly important as the university encourages students, faculty, and staff to use AI tools to improve productivity and the broader campus experience. Rhoden wants to support that adoption without allowing sensitive university information to fall into the wrong hands. One concern is employees signing up for free AI accounts and entering student records, personal information, or other confidential material into services that may use conversations to train or improve their models. Because these tools are readily available, employees without an IT or security background may inadvertently expose information without realizing the implications.

"What scares me most is just how embedded AI has become in everyone's lives," he says. "It's how accessible these tools are, how easy they are to use, and how tempting it is to turn to them and say, 'I could spend time figuring this out, but I could also just get it done in a minute while I'm working on something else.'"

Rhoden sees the work with Lightbeam as an important foundation for managing that risk. With a better understanding of what information the university holds and how sensitive it is, his team can begin drawing clearer boundaries around AI use, distinguishing data that can safely be shared with AI applications from information that should remain off-limits.

Southeastern's work with Lightbeam reflects a broader shift in data security from simply finding sensitive information to understanding it in context, says Himanshu Shukla, co-founder and CEO of Lightbeam. Traditional discovery tools often focus on identifying data such as Social Security numbers or other personally identifiable information, but that alone offers an incomplete picture of risk, he says. For example, identifying a Social Security number in isolation, without understanding whose it is, where it resides, or how it is being used, provides incomplete context for assessing risk.

Building an entity-centric view of data allows organizations like Southeastern to map information scattered across different systems to the associated individuals and organizations, Shukla says. This can enable a more complete picture of what data they hold, where it resides, who can access it, and how it is being shared or used. That context can help security teams identify unnecessary exposure, tighten permissions, and apply more targeted retention, data-handling and automated workflow policies, he notes.

Meanwhile, Rhoden's advice to other universities considering a DSPM investment is to assess both the complexity of their data environments and the resources available to manage them. Universities need to consider whether they have the personnel to manually examine their many data sources and configure the necessary security controls or whether a platform can help automate discovery and provide a more comprehensive view.

"You can't solve problems you don't know exist," Rhoden says. "Once you know what's out there and what problems do exist, you can start planning to solve them."

Improving data security takes time, organizational buy-in, and sustained effort, but establishing visibility, he says, is the essential first step.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9732. 'God Mode' Flaws Could Wreak Border-Control Havoc

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Attackers could have disrupted traveler entry into Nigeria, Ethiopia, Zambia, Sri Lanka, Fiji, and Ghana via several vulnerabilities in their online visa and immigration systems.

Imagine trying to enter a country you've always wanted to visit, only to find yourself not only denied entry but potentially arrested because you've mistakenly ended up on a list of known terrorists.

This is one of several scenarios that could have unfolded if attackers had exploited flaws that independent security researcher Eaton Zveare discovered in the online passport and border-control systems of several countries: Nigeria, Ethiopia, Fiji, Zambia, Sri Lanka, and Ghana.

Though specific to each system, the flaws generally allowed unauthorized access to millions of travelers' sensitive visa and passport data — potentially including biometric information such as fingerprints — and, in some cases, even granted access to administrative functions that could be used to approve or deny entry into a country.

Specifically, Zveare discovered critical API vulnerabilities, including broken object-level authorization (BOLA), broken function-level authorization (BFLA), and missing authentication, in online systems these countries use to process visa applications and authorize travelers to enter.

Related:Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Many of the systems were built by third-party contractors with varying levels of expertise, which likely contributed to the relatively simple and easily avoidable security gaps, Zveare tells Dark Reading. In Nigeria's case, an over-reliance on AI to build the systems may also have introduced flaws into the code.

"I think they've gotten on the AI hype train, and they've kind of used it to build their border control a little bit," he says.

Taken together, the vulnerabilities — which should never exist in "the systems that are vital to national security" — highlight a broader failure to secure critical national infrastructure, potentially with significant consequences for people traveling to these countries, Zveare says.

"The tip of the iceberg is not only viewing all the people who ever applied for these visas and passports, but actually being able to approve or deny applications that are currently coming in," he says, describing the potential for bad actors to exploit the flaws.

Zveare describes the level of access the flaws could provide as "God mode at the border" — also the title of a session he will lead at Black Hat Europe next month about his findings. By exploiting the vulnerabilities, attackers could effectively "have the master key to these countries and their borders," potentially threatening the safety of both citizens and people entering the country. Zveare will disclose the details of the flaws during his session, which is scheduled for Dec. 10.

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

The discovery began almost by accident, when Zveare searched Microsoft Bing for the phrase "admin panel" about a year ago. One of the results led him to a private back-end portal belonging to Nigeria.

After investigating the portal, Zveare uncovered security flaws that gave him access to sensitive immigration systems. Intrigued by what he had found, he began looking for similar systems in other countries, focusing on online passport-control and visa platforms built using modern Web technologies such as Angular and React.

His search eventually led him to five more countries, where he discovered a range of vulnerabilities, including missing authentication and broken access controls — the kinds of common Web flaws that you often see but ones that "you just can't have in critical systems like this," Zveare tells Dark Reading.

In Nigeria alone, Zveare identified roughly a dozen vulnerabilities, while the other countries had several each. He went on to develop exploits to demonstrate how the flaws could allow an attacker not only to view sensitive personally identifiable information (PII) belonging to visa applicants, but also to access administrative functions that could determine whether someone was granted entry into a country.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

The potential consequences extend well beyond disrupted travel plans and compromised personal information, Zveare says. One worst-case scenario would involve an attacker identifying a high-level executive or other person of interest who might be targeted for kidnapping or assassination, then accessing their travel itinerary, hotel information, and other details that could be used to track their movements.

"You would know exactly when they land, where they are staying, and how long they're staying," Zveare says. "I'm sure you can imagine what bad people could do with that info."

Because the systems were spread across multiple foreign countries, many of which rely on outside companies to build their online infrastructure, identifying the parties responsible for fixing the vulnerabilities proved trickier than a typical bug disclosure, Zveare says.

"So all these countries have their computer emergency response teams (CERTs)," he tells Dark Reading. "Unfortunately, a lot of them did not respond."

One country whose response was particularly strong was also the one whose systems had the most problems: Nigeria, which moved quickly to resolve the vulnerabilities. Its response team had "a generally excellent response," Zveare says.

Indeed, Nigeria is emerging as "the big tech hub of Africa," and he expected its authorities to be relatively on top of these issues, he says.

When a country's CERT failed to respond, Zveare had to dig deeper to identify the independent contractor that had built the system and contact the company directly. In many cases, this proved to be the quickest route to remediation.

Overall, response times ranged from a few days to more than six months. By now, however, "everything is pretty much fixed," he says.

While Zveare says all the contractors he contacted were helpful and responsive in addressing the vulnerabilities, their security practices may have contributed to the problems in the first place.

"[The contractors] might have come in at the lowest bid, and that's what the country went with," Zveare says. "I feel as though, with how simple some of these flaws were, they might not have the most sophisticated security reviews."

One quick test Zveare uses when assessing a Web API is to look for an administrative endpoint that retrieves a list of all users. "So I'll uncover that, and I'll just copy that endpoint into my browser and see what happens."

In the case of the vulnerable border-control systems, "a lot of the time, they would just return the entire users list because they don't check for the authentication token," he says.

The problems went beyond improper token handling, however. In some cases, authentication tokens were missing altogether, meaning sensitive endpoints could be accessed without the required authentication.

This lack of fundamental Web security points to a broader failure of oversight by national authorities when selecting the contractors entrusted with building and maintaining their systems, Zveare says. For infrastructure as sensitive as border control systems, that lack of scrutiny is not only unacceptable but potentially dangerous.

"You have to properly vet these contractors because you're giving your nation's security to them," Zveare says. "And if they don't know basic Web security, you're going to have a bad time."

#9731. Webworm APT Slithers Into Networks With Customized SoftEther VPN

The China-aligned espionage group rebuilt the open source VPN software from source, stripping out the artifacts that would normally expose it to defenders.

An infamous cyber-espionage group has added a new trick to its tool belt, in the form of VPN bridge obfuscation.

Rapid7 published research concerning Webworm, a China-aligned advanced persistent threat (APT) group first reported on in 2022 and believed to be active since at least 2017. Webworm's activity predominantly targets government organizations, with an emphasis on Europe. The group has also been tracked as Erudite Mogwai and Space Pirates.

Webworm has been known to deploy the open source SoftEther VPN on previously compromised government networks. While SoftEther is a legitimate multiprotocol VPN, threat actors abuse its capabilities in attacks. Webworm actors in particular include a "VPN Bridge" component allowing them to link a victim's internal network directly to attacker-controlled servers to facilitate long-term access.

The new research, published on Nov. 19, covers what Rapid7 researcher and blog post author Milan Spinka called "a so-far unknown custom SoftEther-based tool, which implements various tricks to hide itself from security tools, and which we attribute to Webworm with moderate confidence."

Related:'TheMailer' Phishing Kit Puts AI in the Driver's Seat

Rapid7 has identified a range of samples of the tool, which is internally described as "NtMonitor." The tool is a modified build of SoftEther VPN Bridge compiled for Windows x64 and appears to be specifically designed to disguise legitimate SoftEther VPN software as a benign network monitoring utility so the attacker can maintain long-term, stealthy access to a compromised network while evading detection tools made to recognize standard SoftEther software artifacts.

At its core, Spinka wrote, it appears the attacker "methodically analyzed SoftEther's detection surface and implemented countermeasures to all of the easy ways a detection engineer may target it."

Attackers changed the metadata and internal branding to refer to generic "Network Monitor Software," for example. Additionally, they changed internal string references to refer to "NtMonitor VPN" like debug banners, service names, registry pages, and firewall rule names (though this was inconsistently applied); renamed the HTTP endpoints used by the VPN protocol; changed the handshake watermark so standard SoftEther detection signatures wouldn't pick it up; stripped down a core file (hamcore.se2) and embedded it inside the executable; and renamed and encrypted SoftEther's plaintext configuration file with a custom cipher.

Rapid7 attributed the software to Webworm with moderate confidence, due to alignment with previously reported Webworm tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs), as well as remote IP addresses traced to infrastructure repeatedly linked to Webworm activity in the past. Rapid7's research blog includes indicators of compromise and YARA rules for defenders.

Related:Anthropic Finds Ingredients for Future AI Worms

Dark Reading contacted Rapid7 for additional information, but the research team was unavailable at press time.

One of Webworm's primary initial access methods appears to be exploiting vulnerabilities through external Web-facing applications, based on prior vendor research and the APT's affinity for vulnerability scanner Nuclei. Defenders wary of Webworm should prioritize internet-facing patching, Web Application Firewall (WAF) enforcement, and strict network egress controls.

#9730. Same Product, Different Price: What an AI Shopping Agent Learned From 24,394 Items

Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.

Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.

Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.

Finding prices is easy. Proving two listings are the same product is the hard part.

Ask any AI shopping agent to find the best price and it will happily return one. The harder question is whether that price is for the same thing. A vacuum listed at two stores can differ by model year, bundle or pack size, and a price comparison that misses that is worse than none at all.

Deal.ai, an AI shopping agent built by Famous Labs, has been measuring both problems: how much prices really differ for identical products, and how hard it is to know two listings are identical in the first place.

From October 29 to November 4, 2026, Deal.ai compared 24,394 new products sold at two or more of 16 major U.S. retailers, including Amazon, Walmart, Target and Best Buy. Each store's price had to be read within an hour of the others.

The results were consistent. About two in three products had prices at least 5% apart across the big retailers. Among the 4,684 products sold at four or more retailers, a shopper who checked one store picked at random paid, on average, 15.6% above the lowest listed price. Checking two stores cut that to 7.4%, three stores to 3.7%, and four to 1.1%.

The biggest names were not always cheapest. At the same moment, another big retailer listed the item for less 37% of the time for Walmart products, 34% for Amazon, 41% for Best Buy and 51% for Target.

Those numbers only mean something if every price is for the same item. Deal.ai's answer is to separate matching from pricing.

In a live recheck on November 5, Deal.ai drew 600 products at random and kept the ones with a brand and a model number or barcode. A separate AI model then read each store's own listing title, with prices hidden, and kept only listings that were the identical item: same model, size, capacity, pack count and generation. Colour could differ; bundles, refurbished and open-box listings could not.

Of 4,990 store listings, 1,886 passed. That is a strict filter by design. It throws away near-matches that a looser system would happily compare, which keeps a "lower price" from really being a smaller pack or last year's model. Hiding prices from the matching model matters too: it stops the model from being swayed toward a match by a price that looks plausible.

"Finding prices is the easy part. The hard part is making sure every store is selling the exact same product, the same model and the same size," said Alex Mehr, Ph.D., co-founder and CEO of Famous Labs, the company behind Deal.ai. "That's what our agents are built to check, so shoppers can trust the price comparison they see."

Deal.ai puts that work behind a simple interface. Shoppers ask for what they want in plain English, and the agent researches the options, compares live prices across thousands of stores and sends them to the store with the best deal. Its agents also run every hour to surface unusually good deals, each with a deal score out of 10. A free deal checker takes a link to any deal and finds the same item at every big store.

For developers, Deal.ai also offers an MCP server, so other AI assistants can call it directly instead of scraping stores themselves.

Price data is abundant. Trustworthy comparisons are not. The gap between one store and the best price is large enough to matter to shoppers, but only if the agent is honest about which listings truly match. Strict matching, with prices hidden from the matcher, is a simple rule that makes every number after it more believable.

Deal.ai is free at deal.ai. The full study is published on Deal.ai's research page.

#9729. Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!

Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.

In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.

This post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.

Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.

A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.

For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:

MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d

Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.

The useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.

HierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.

These merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.

You can make compression proportional to document length:

With pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.

HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:

This distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.

Adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.

Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:

Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.

Pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.

If you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.

For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:

L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​

The first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives update the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.

Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:

CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.

Gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.

The poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.

Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.

The complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:

The script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.

You can also train on a cloud GPU with Hugging Face Jobs. Install the CLI and log in with a token that can run Jobs and upload models:

This runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.

You can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:

In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:

Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.

Sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.

The default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.

Let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:

The pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.

You can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).

To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:

Both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.

I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.

For adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.

At the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.

The gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.

If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:

If the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.

MultiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.

Try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.

With a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!

#9728. What Happier People Tend To Believe About Others

A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

Trusting others is linked to greater happiness and life satisfaction, a review involving over 2.5 million people finds.

Happier people also tend to become more trusting over time.

The link between trust and happiness is slightly stronger in children, adolescents and older adults, possibly because supportive relationships are especially important at these ages.

Trust may help meet the need to belong by making it easier to build relationships in which people feel supported and secure.

The research combined almost 1,000 findings from studies involving people aged six to 84.

The analysis examined how trust related to everyday emotions, including happiness and sadness, as well as people’s overall satisfaction with their lives.

Greater trust was consistently associated with better wellbeing.

The association was somewhat stronger among children and adolescents than among young and middle-aged adults, and stronger among older adults than young adults.

Trust may matter more at ages when people are building close relationships or becoming more dependent on others.

For younger people, learning whom to trust is part of building meaningful friendships and supportive social networks.

In later life, people may prioritise a smaller circle of close relationships and depend more on others for support.

The researchers distinguished between trust in familiar people, trust in people generally and trust in institutions.

The first involves confidence in someone known personally, such as a partner, friend or relative.

General trust involves expectations about people more broadly, including strangers, while institutional trust concerns organisations such as governments, banks and the police.

All three were associated with better wellbeing, but trust in familiar people showed the strongest connection.

Trust may support wellbeing partly because close relationships require a willingness to be vulnerable.

Expecting someone to respond with care can make it easier to seek help, cooperate and maintain a supportive connection.

These relationships may satisfy the basic psychological need to feel connected to others and cared for in return.

Trust could also provide a broader sense of security and predictability, making the social world feel more dependable.

This may help explain why trust was slightly more closely related to overall life satisfaction than to positive or negative emotions.

Life satisfaction reflects a broader assessment of how life is going, whereas emotions can fluctuate with immediate experiences.

The relationship also worked in the other direction, with greater wellbeing predicting more trust later.

One proposed explanation is that emotions influence how people interpret the world around them.

Feeling happy may encourage more positive perceptions of other people, while anxiety may draw attention towards threats and uncertainty.

Trust and wellbeing could therefore reinforce each other, with supportive expectations helping people feel better and positive feelings making trust easier.

The wider social environment mattered too, with a stronger connection between trust and wellbeing in countries where people were generally more trusting.

A trusting outlook may be more beneficial when the people around us are dependable.

Simply encouraging someone to trust more overlooks the behaviour of the people and institutions receiving that trust.

Professor Catrin Finkenauer, study co-author, said:

“But trust can’t be forced—it has to be earned.”

The findings therefore highlight the importance of honesty, reliability, transparency and fair treatment in relationships and institutions.

“When we build trust, we also support mental health and stronger communities.”

The study was published in the journal Psychological Bulletin (Bi et al., 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean
